six open; three settled (A084703, A155543, A111403) and the other three are out of reach
for the reasons given in the m-section note above section 4. Roots of unity were never needed — both sides' posted
closed forms decided each one.

~~`xref.py`~~ — SWEPT. It settled exactly one entry, A052183, already in the roster. The
triangle references `A######(n,k)` -- another 21 -- still need the triangle's own formula
first, and remain untried.

Word-counting entries ("binary strings of length n with equally many 001 and 010") are a
recognisable family among the 268 unreadable ones, and they are not out of reach: a
transfer matrix in two variables gives a rational `R(x,u)`, the sequence is
`[x^n][u^0]R`, and a diagonal of a bivariate rational function is algebraic. Not attempted.

~~The second Lagrange form~~ — DEAD, measured 31 Aug 2026. The shape exists but carries no
conjectured recurrences anywhere; see the note above section 4.


### 2 Sep 2026: the refusal census, redone — 35 papers from the K X K subblock matrices

Two checks this round. The first was a null and is recorded as one: `sweep_ord.py` skips
roster entries, exactly as the table sweep did, so an entry already papered by another
engine could be carrying an unclaimed `Empirical recurrence of order N` line. It is not.
All 68 roster entries that carry such a line are the 68 order-recovery papers themselves.
Nothing to fix, no papers, and the `SKIP_ROSTER` switch is now on that sweep too so the
question can be re-asked in one command.

The second was the refusal census done again from scratch — every non-roster entry whose
name mentions an array and which carries a parsable conjectured recurrence that no engine
reads. **723 entries**, clustered by the opening of the condition rather than by the whole
name. The clusters are real families, not a long tail:

| entries | family |
|---|---|
| ~99 | `(n+K-1) X W 0..m matrices with each K X K subblock idempotent / of equal population / of equal permanent` |
| ~80 | `ways to reciprocally link elements of an n X W array …` |
| ~100 | `Hilltop / Equals one / Unmatched value / Sum of neighbor / Majority value maps` |
| ~40 | `0..k colorings of a W X (n+1) array circular in the n+1 direction` |
| ~40 | `arrays of the minimum value of corresponding elements and their neighbors` |

The first two families are now closed: `transfer23.py`, **35 papers**, and
`transfer24.py`, **76 papers** — the whole reciprocal-link family, every entry of it that
carries a conjectured recurrence.

**Why it needed more than the existing engines.** The condition ties together K consecutive
ROWS and K consecutive COLUMNS at once, so one row is not a state; the state is the strip of
the last K-1 rows, of which there are `(m+1)^((K-1)W)` — 2^18 at K=3, W=9, and out of reach
past that. They are not enumerated. Two consecutive K X K windows of a K X W band overlap in
K X (K-1), so a band is a walk in the overlap graph on the admissible windows, and the states
are exactly the tops and bottoms of bands. That turns a search over strips into a search over
windows. The state counts that come out are tiny: 8, 36, 416, 1905 where the naive count is
astronomically larger.

**The idempotent windows needed a theorem.** Sifting all `2^(K*K)` matrices is already
awkward at K=6 and hopeless past it. Writing `B^2 = B` row by row says each row is the sum of
the rows indexed by its own support, and comparing supports gives a closed description of the
0-1 idempotents — pick the zero rows Z, pick the primitive indices B* with `r_b = e_b + (a
subset of Z)`, and let every other nonzero row be a disjoint union of those. It generates each
one exactly once. Counts: 8, 50, 452, 5682, 96608 for K = 2..6, and the first three agree with
exhaustion over all `2^(K*K)` matrices. That agreement is the check that the description is
neither too wide nor too narrow; the lemma and its proof are in every paper of the family.

**The two "all equal" conditions split.** `having the same population` and `permanent equal`
do not name the common value. Fix v, count the matrices all of whose windows have that value,
and the sets for different v are disjoint because the value is determined by the matrix. A
disjoint union of the per-v digraphs counts the whole thing with the same all-ones vectors.

**Verification.** Beyond the usual three checks, the model was re-derived independently: a
direct brute-force count straight from the definition, enumerating every matrix of the small
sizes and testing every window, for eight entries covering all three conditions and the
alphabets 0..1, 0..2 and 0..3. Every one matched the published DATA. The audit of the 35
papers reports no problems.

**What is left in this family.** K = 6, 7, 8 idempotent (about 20 entries): the windows can be
generated but there are 96608 of them at K = 6 and 2.2 million at K = 7, so the graph is far
past the size at which the annihilation test is affordable here. The square `(n+K-1) X (n+K-1)`
entries are not a walk in one parameter and are refused, as always. A few wide population
entries are over the state cap. Recorded, not pending.

All five families in the table above have now been worked.

### 2 Sep 2026, same day: the reciprocal-link family — 76 papers, the whole family

`Number of ways to reciprocally link elements of an n X W array either to themselves or to
exactly one/two <neighbours> neighbors[, without 3-loops | without consecutive collinear
links]`. 76 entries in the refusal census, and all 76 are now papers.

**The modelling step is the whole difficulty; after it the engine is small.** A link is
reciprocal, so it is an undirected EDGE, and "linked to itself" means "in no edge". So the
entry counts the spanning subgraphs of a grid graph whose every vertex has degree 0 or d:
matchings for d = 1, disjoint unions of cycles for d = 2. Every neighbour offset moves the row
index by at most one, so the set of edges crossing one row boundary is a state, and placing a
row settles the degree of each of its cells once and for all.

**Two readings had to be fixed, not guessed.**
- Can a cell spend both links on the same neighbour? No. For king moves the 1 X 2 and 2 X 2
  counts are the degree-0-or-2 subgraphs of `K_2` and `K_4`, which are 1 and 1+4+3 = 8 with
  simple edges and more with a doubled edge; the entries publish 1 and 8.
- `without 3-loops` is triangles, not doubled edges — and it was nearly misread as `2-loops`
  from a digit-collapsed cluster listing. Three cells pairwise adjacent always lie in two
  consecutive rows (three in one row cannot be pairwise adjacent, the outer two being two
  columns apart), so carrying the previous row's horizontal edges in the state catches every
  one.
- `without consecutive collinear links` forbids a vertex whose two links are opposite. It is a
  condition on one vertex, decided where the degree is.

**State counts are tiny** — 5 to 40 — because the degree bound prunes the boundary hard. The
whole family cost one sweep.

**Verification.** Besides the usual three, the model was re-derived independently: a brute
force over every subset of the edge set, straight from the definition, for 12 entries covering
d = 1 and d = 2, both flags, both orientations and four neighbour sets. All matched. The audit
of the 76 reports no problems.

Ten entries of the family parse but carry no recurrence a parser reads; nothing is claimed for
them.

### 2 Sep 2026, third family: circular colourings — 41 of 43

`Number of 0..m colorings of an n X W array circular in the W direction with new values 0..m
introduced in row major order`, and the same with the array written `R X (n+c)` and circular
in the growing direction. 43 entries; 41 are now papers.

**The reading.** A colouring is proper — adjacent cells differ — and "circular in the W
direction" joins the two ends of that direction. Confirmed by the entries' own first terms: a
cycle of 6 cells has `2^6 + 2 = 66` proper 3-colourings and `66/3! = 11` is what the one-row
entry publishes.

**The relabelling clause is transfer20's argument unchanged**: what is counted is patterns,
`L_i = sum_j N_j i(i-1)...(i-j+1)` is triangular, and `a = (1^T F^-1) L`.

**The two circular directions are not the same problem.**
- Circular ACROSS the walk: a row is a proper colouring of `C_W`, consecutive rows differ
  everywhere, `L_i(n)` is an ordinary walk count.
- Circular ALONG the walk: a column is a proper colouring of `P_R` and `L_i(m) = tr(T^m)`. A
  trace is not `iota^T M^m tau`, and one walk per starting vertex is unaffordable. It is not
  needed: `T` commutes with permuting the colours, so the diagonal entry depends only on the
  colouring's equality pattern, and `tr(T^m)` is a weighted sum of a handful of closed-walk
  counts, one per pattern.

**The lumping is what made it affordable, and it was the difference between 24 and 41.** The
first sweep proved 24 and left 19 over the cap or timed out. Everything in sight commutes with
permuting the colours, so a walk started at a symmetric vector may be run on the ORBITS. The
state counts collapse: 994 to 16, 1062 to 281, and two entries that had been over the cap came
in at 318 and 59. Storing the lumped adjacency with multiplicities instead of repeated targets
cut the matrix-vector cost again, and that took it to 41.

**Verification.** Besides the usual three, an independent brute force enumerating every array
over the alphabet and testing properness and the row-major canonical form, for 9 entries across
both circular directions and alphabets 3..8. All matched. The audit of the 41 reports no
problems.

**The two left**: A214116 and A214170, mode B with 4761 and 2544 orbit states; the residual
test is still too slow here. Recorded, not pending.

### 2 Sep 2026, fourth family: the `maps' entries — 114 of 164, and the first IMAGE count

`<Family> maps: number of n X W binary arrays indicating the locations of corresponding
elements <condition> in a random 0..m n X W array`, for seven families: Hilltop (`not exceeded
by any`), Unmatched value (`not equal to any`), Unchanging value (`unequal to no`, i.e. equal
to every), Majority value, Equals one, Equals two and Sum of neighbor (`equal to the sum mod k
of`). 164 entries in the refusal census; 114 are now papers.

**This is a different KIND of count and it is why the family had sat there.** Every other
engine counts objects satisfying a condition. These count the IMAGE of a map: how many
different indicator arrays arise as the 0..m array runs over all its values. Two different
arrays with the same marking must be counted once, so no walk count on the arrays gives the
answer.

**The cure is the subset construction.** A cell's marking depends on the rows above, at and
below it, so the pair of the last two rows read is the state of a nondeterministic machine
whose OUTPUT is the indicator array; the distinct outputs are the paths of its determinisation,
whose states are the sets of pairs still consistent with what has been emitted. Those sets are
generated from the start set outward and there are few of them — 8 to a few thousand.

One detail is easy to get wrong and is proved rather than assumed: the LAST marked row is
emitted with nothing below it, so it is not a step of the walk. It is a count attached to the
state the walk stops in — the number of distinct final rows that state still admits — so the
end vector is not the all-ones vector. The lemma in every paper of the family states the
invariant of the subset construction and derives `a(n) = iota^T M^(n-1) tau` from it.

**Verification.** Besides the usual three, an independent brute force that builds every array,
marks it and counts the distinct markings, for 14 entries covering all seven families, both
orientations and alphabets 0..1 to 0..3. All matched. The audit of the 114 reports no problems.

**Left**: 50 entries over the subset cap of 20000 or too slow for the residual test here —
mostly Hilltop at the wider widths. Recorded, not pending.

Ranked at tier 4. The reduction is a real one with its own lemma, but the subset construction
is textbook, so it is not ranked with the bespoke arguments.

### 2 Sep 2026, fifth family: two more image counts — 55 of 62

The last family the refusal census listed, and it splits in two, both image counts, both
settled by the same determinisation. The subset construction is now factored out into
`imagedet.py` and shared, so the three engines that use it cannot drift apart.

- `Number of n X W arrays of the MINIMUM value of corresponding elements and their
  <neighbours> in a random 0..m n X W array` — 43 entries, 40 proved. Each derived cell holds
  the least of its own value and its neighbours'; the row window is three rows, as in the
  `maps` families, so the last derived row is again counted at the state the walk stops in.
- `Number of n X W 0..k arrays of the MEDIAN (or SUM) of the corresponding element, the
  element to the east and the element to the south in a larger (n+1) X (W+1) 0..m array` —
  17 entries, 15 proved. Here the derived cell reads two consecutive rows only, so the state
  is a single row and there is no final emission: the walk simply has n steps. Some of these
  add `without adjacent equal elements in the latter`, which removes transitions and start
  states and nothing else. The stated output alphabet is checked against the operation
  (3m for a sum, m for a median) and a name that disagrees is refused rather than guessed at.

**Verification.** An independent brute force building every array, applying the operation and
counting distinct results, for 10 entries across both shapes, both operations and the
`without adjacent equal` variant. All matched. The audit of the 55 reports no problems.

**Left**: 7 entries — 3 over the subset cap at the wider widths, 2 sums at width 5 and 7, and
the 2 `minimum or maximum` entries, whose English is genuinely ambiguous (a per-cell choice
between the two fits the first terms, but I have not pinned it and will not count a guess).

With this the five families the census found stand at 35+76+41+114+55 = **321 papers**, out of
the 723 entries it listed.

### 2 Sep 2026: the census redone over the WHOLE corpus — 3667 left, and two more families

The first census only looked at names containing `array`, `grid` or `matri`. Redone over every
entry: **3667 non-roster entries carry a conjectured recurrence that no engine reads**, in 498
distinct shapes. The five families already worked were the visible top of it. Two more are now
done, 175 papers.

**Order statistics of every 2 X 2 subblock, all equal — 99 of 101.**
`Number of (n+1)X(K+1) 0..m arrays with <the maximum plus the upper median minus the lower
median minus the minimum> of every 2X2 subblock equal.` Sorting a subblock's four entries as
a<=b<=c<=d names them minimum, lower median, upper median, maximum, and the entries take every
signed sum of those four. The common value is not named, so the count splits by it exactly as
in the idempotent family; for a fixed value the condition is two rows wide and a row is a
state.

**`Colored with' — 76 of 88 — and what it actually means.**
`Number of (n+1)X(K+1) 0..2 arrays colored with the upper median value of each 2X2 subblock.`
The name gives no condition at all on its face, and that is why it had never been read. It is
a PROPER COLOURING: the subblocks form an n X K grid, each is coloured by the statistic, and
neighbouring subblocks — horizontally and vertically — must differ.

The reading was pinned numerically before anything was built. For the upper median over 0..2:
a 2X2 array has one subblock and no neighbouring pair, so all 81 arrays qualify; a 2X3 array
has one pair and 294 of 729 qualify; a 3X3 array has four pairs and 722 qualify. Those are the
three numbers the entries publish. No condition would give 729 at 2X3; counting the diagonal
pairs as neighbours too would give 0 at 3X3. Neither is what is meant. The justification is in
every paper of the family.

Here the state has to be a PAIR of consecutive array rows, not a row: a subblock's colour needs
two rows, and the vertical condition compares two subblock rows. Some of these colour by the
SET of distinct values in the subblock rather than by a number, which the same machinery
handles unchanged.

**Verification.** Independent brute force from the definition for 16 entries across both
families, every colour kind including the set-valued one, and several widths. All matched. The
audit of the 175 reports no problems.

**Left**: 2 of the `equal` entries and 12 of the `colored` ones, over the state cap at the
wider widths, plus the 5 `colored ... with new values introduced row-major order` entries,
which stack the relabelling reduction on top and were not attempted. The square
`(n+1)X(n+1)` entries are refused as always.

### 2 Sep 2026: monotone subblock statistics — 84 papers

`Number of (n+1)X(K+1) 0..m arrays with every 2X2 subblock <statistic> nondecreasing
horizontally, vertically and ne-to-sw antidiagonally.` The subblocks form a grid, each carries
the value of a statistic of its four entries, and the value must not decrease along the named
directions of that grid. Some entries name TWO statistics, one for the horizontal direction
and one for the vertical; both are functions of the same subblock, so both are read off the
same pair of rows.

Every direction moves the subblock row by at most one, so the state is a pair of consecutive
array rows — that pair fixes a whole subblock row — and one step settles every comparison
between two consecutive subblock rows.

**Three readings were pinned numerically before anything was built.**
- `ne-to-sw antidiagonally` is the offset (+1,-1) on the subblock grid. The offset (+1,+1)
  gives 164 where the entry publishes 126.
- `diagonal minus antidiagonal sum` is (p+s)-(q+r).
- `ne-sw antidiagonal difference` is q-r, and `nw+se diagonal sum` is p+s.
Each was settled by counting the small arrays directly. The justification is in every paper.

Transposed names (`(K+1)X(n+1)`) swap the two coordinates of every direction; a direction that
then points upward is turned round by reversing its inequality, which is done in the parser
rather than left to chance. Square `(n+1)X(n+1)` entries are refused as always.

**Verification.** Independent brute force from the definition for 10 entries. All matched.
The audit of the 84 reports no problems.

**The rest of this family is 3 X 3.** About 120 more entries use the same grammar over
3 X 3 subblocks, where the statistics are built from the diagonal, the antidiagonal, the
central row and the central column (`sum of the medians of the diagonal and antidiagonal minus
the two sums of the central row and column`). The transfer is the same shape with a state of
three consecutive rows; only the statistic parser is missing. Not done, and recorded as the
obvious next step rather than as a wall.

### 2 Sep 2026: the 3 X 3 half of the monotone family — 110 papers

The same grammar over 3 X 3 subblocks. A 3 X 3 subblock has four distinguished lines of three
cells — diagonal, antidiagonal, central row, central column — and the statistic is a signed sum
of aggregates (sum, maximum, minimum, median) over those lines: `sum of the medians of the
diagonal and antidiagonal minus the two sums of the central row and column'. All 154 such
names parse; 110 are settled, the rest are over the state cap.

**The state had to be compressed to reach the wider arrays.** A 3 X 3 subblock spans three
array rows and the vertical comparison spans four, so the obvious state is three consecutive
rows — 2^(3W), out of reach past W = 4. It is not needed. What a step consults is the last TWO
rows, enough to build the next subblock row when one more arrives, and the PREVIOUS SUBBLOCK
ROW to compare against. Carrying the subblock row instead of the third array row collapses all
third rows giving the same statistics into one state, and the starting vector becomes weighted
— one unit per first row that produces the state. At W = 5 that is 5376 states instead of
32768, and the whole family came within reach.

A parser bug found on the way: `... nonincreasing horizontally and nondecreasing vertically'
names the statistic once and changes only the RELATION. The clause splitter assumed every
relation word was preceded by its own statistic and refused those names outright. Fixed in both
the 2 X 2 and 3 X 3 engines; it was worth 3 entries in the first and a share of the second.

### 2 Sep 2026: a LaTeX audit of the whole roster — 452 papers had broken math

Checking the build logs of the newest papers for errors turned up a display-math bug, and
running the same check over every build log in the tree found it was not new. **452 papers
already in the roster compiled with LaTeX errors** and were carrying visibly wrong output.
Four distinct causes:

| papers | fault |
|---|---|
| 343 | a sentence about the scale factor printed an empty `$$` when the factor was 1, which opens display math and derails the rest of the proof |
| 59 + 24 | the extra state component was emitted after the closing `$`, so `\times \{0,..,1\}` sat in text mode |
| 26 | a stored formula string had `\le` running straight into the next symbol, read as the control sequence `\lex`; and `\times` inside `\text{...}` |
| 424 (this round, caught before delivery) | offsets written as `$(0,1)$, $(1,0)$` INSIDE a `\[...\]`, and in one family a stray backslash before the whole list |

All are fixed in the builders, all 452 rebuilt and recompiled clean, and the PDFs replaced in
place. No paper's mathematics changed and the count is unaffected — this is a presentation
defect, not a proof defect — but 452 delivered papers had a visible one and the check that
would have caught it was not being run. **`grep '^! ' build/*/p.log` is now part of the routine
after every build.**

### 2 Sep 2026: differing by exactly one — 91 papers

`Number of (n+1)X(K+1) 0..m arrays with <an order statistic expression> of every 2X2 subblock
differing from its horizontal and vertical neighbors by EXACTLY ONE.` 105 entries of this exact
shape; 91 settled, the rest square or over the cap.

Same subblock grid and same statistic vocabulary as the `colored with' family, with a sharper
relation: neighbouring values must differ by exactly d, not merely differ. The state is again a
pair of consecutive array rows.

Each paper checks its own first term against the shape of the grid: at width 2 a single
subblock has no neighbour at all, so a(1) must be the full count of 2x2 arrays over the
alphabet, and the entries publish exactly that. The papers that came out at two pages were
short of that remark; adding it is content, not padding, and all 91 are three pages.

**The 2 X 2 subblock pool is still large.** 856 refused entries carry a 2 X 2 subblock clause.
The shapes now settled are the order-statistic ones. What remains, with counts:
commuting with the neighbouring subblock (48 at 2 X 2, ~60 more at 3 X 3 and 4 X 4), singular
and nonsingular (26), determinant/permanent/trace equal to or differing from a neighbour's
(~45), `number of clockwise edge increases' and its relatives (~90), `nondecreasing rightwards
and downwards' for determinants and permanents (~30), and lexicographic row/column comparisons
(~25). The first three need only a wider statistic vocabulary in an engine of the shape already
written; the edge-increase family needs its definition pinned against data first, and the
lexicographic one needs a comparison state carried per adjacent column pair.

### 2 Sep 2026: determinant, permanent, trace — 94 papers

Four shapes, one engine, all over the 2 X 2 subblocks of an (n+1) X W array:

| shape | state |
|---|---|
| `every 2X2 subblock singular / nonsingular` | one row |
| `the <stat>s of all 2X2 subblocks equal [and nonzero]` | one row, split by the unnamed common value |
| `no 2X2 subblock <stat> equal to any horizontal or vertical neighbour's` | a pair of rows |
| `the <stat>s of 2X2 subblocks nondecreasing rightwards and downwards` | a pair of rows |

The state shape follows from whether the condition looks at ONE subblock or at a NEIGHBOURING
PAIR, and the parser records which. That distinction is the whole design: a per-subblock
condition needs only a row, a neighbour condition needs the pair of rows that produces two
subblock rows.

**Verification.** Independent brute force from the definition for 10 entries across all four
shapes. All matched. The audit reports no problems, and the build logs are clean.

**A note on paper length.** The first build of this family and the last came out at two pages,
short of the house minimum of three. Rather than pad, two real remarks were added: what the
first term must be from the shape of the grid alone (and that the entry publishes exactly
that), and the range the statistic can take over the alphabet, which is the bound that keeps
the split-by-value construction finite. All 94 are three pages.

**Still open in this pool**: `commuting with the neighbouring subblock' (about 108 across
2 X 2, 3 X 3 and 4 X 4 — the state is K consecutive rows, so only K = 2 and narrow K = 3 are
affordable), `equal to SOME neighbour' and `equal to exactly one or two neighbours' (about 20 —
these are not pairwise-local, since a subblock's condition is only settled once the row below
exists, so the state needs a per-subblock flag), the `edge increases' statistics (about 90 —
the definition needs pinning against data first), and the lexicographic row/column comparisons
(about 25).

### 2 Sep 2026: commuting subblocks — 35 of 126, and the state that will not compress

`Number of (n+K-1) X W 0..m arrays with every K X K subblock commuting with each horizontal
and vertical neighbor K X K subblock`, together with the `no ... commuting' negation and the
variant that also demands nonzero determinant. 126 entries in the census; **35 settled**.

Neighbouring subblocks OVERLAP — horizontally in K X (K-1) entries, vertically in (K-1) X K —
but each is still a K X K integer matrix, and the condition is AB = BA. A subblock row needs K
consecutive array rows and the vertical comparison needs K+1, so the state is K consecutive
rows.

**This is the first family where the state genuinely does not compress**, and the papers say
so. The trick that rescued the 3 X 3 monotone family — carry the previous subblock ROW instead
of the extra array row — buys nothing here: for W >= K the subblock row already determines the
K array rows it came from. So the size is (m+1)^(KW) before pruning, and that is what puts the
rest of the family out of range.

Of the 91 not settled: **69 over the state cap**, 22 carry no recurrence a parser reads, and 2
build but the residual test does not finish. Reported as a measured wall, not as an unexplored
idea.

**Verification.** Independent brute force from the definition for one entry of each of the six
variants that occur — K = 2, 3, 4, with `every' and with `no', and with the determinant clause.
All matched. Audit clean, build logs clean.

### 2 Sep 2026: edge counts — 86 papers, and three readings pinned before any engine was written

`the number of clockwise edge increases in every 2X2 subblock ...`. 298 entries use one of
these edge counts; 86 of the cleanly-phrased 2 X 2 ones are settled.

**The definitions were measured, not assumed.** Going clockwise round a subblock
`p q / r s` the cycle is p -> q -> s -> r -> p and the count is how many of those four steps go
up; counterclockwise is the same cycle reversed; `rightwards and downwards' counts instead the
four directed edges p->q, r->s, p->r, q->s; `equal edges' counts perimeter edges joining equal
cells. Three independent checks, each computed by direct enumeration before an engine existed:

| check | value | entry publishes |
|---|---|---|
| 2 X 3 binary arrays whose two subblocks have equal clockwise counts | 40 | 40 |
| 2 X 2 arrays over 0..2 with clockwise count 2 | 30 | 30 |
| 3 X 2 binary arrays whose two subblocks have unequal rightwards-and-downwards counts | 40 | 40 |

Those three numbers are quoted in every paper of the family.

Five shapes, two state shapes: `equal to k' (with an optional nonzero-determinant clause),
`clockwise count unequal to counterclockwise count', and `all the same' are conditions on ONE
subblock, so a row is a state; `equal to all its neighbours' and `differing from all its
neighbours' relate NEIGHBOURING subblocks, so the state is a pair of rows.

Verified by brute force from the definition for one entry of each of the five kinds plus five
at random. Audit clean, build logs clean.

**Left in this family**: the `2X3 or 3X2 subblock' variants (about 60 — a different window
shape), the ones carrying a relabelling clause (about 40), and the mixed forms that ask for the
same count horizontally and a different one vertically (about 25).

### 2 Sep 2026: the 2 X 3 / 3 X 2 perimeter cycle — 49 papers

`every 2X3 or 3X2 subblock having exactly two clockwise edge increases`, and its relatives.
112 entries name these two window shapes; 49 settled.

Both shapes have all six cells ON the perimeter, so each carries a 6-cycle: for
`p q / r s / t u` the clockwise cycle is p->q->s->u->t->r->p, and for `p q t / r s u` it is
p->q->t->u->s->r->p. Four readings pinned by direct enumeration before any engine existed:

| check | value | entry publishes |
|---|---|---|
| 3 X 2 over 0..2, clockwise count 2 | 423 | 423 |
| 3 X 2 over 0..2, clockwise count 3 | 150 | 150 |
| 3 X 2 over 0..3, clockwise count 1 | 480 | 480 |
| 2 X 3 over 0..2, clockwise count 2 | 423 | 423 |

**The two window shapes want different amounts of state, and that is the design.** A 2 X 3
window lies inside ONE pair of consecutive rows, so it decides which pairs are admissible at
all; a 3 X 2 window straddles THREE rows, so it decides which pair may follow which. One pair
of rows serves both.

Three conditions occur: an exact count of clockwise or counterclockwise increases; an exact
count of each; and the two counts equal or unequal. Brute force from the definition verified
one entry of each kind plus four at random. Audit clean, build logs clean.

### 2 Sep 2026: relabelling meets the edge counts — 54 papers, and a guard that was wrong

Two pieces. First, 18 more of the plain edge-count family: the MIXED form, which asks for the
same count along one direction and a different one along the other (and sometimes names a
different statistic for each direction), plus the transposed names, where writing the array
with n as the number of COLUMNS exchanges the two directions.

Second, 36 entries counted UP TO RELABELLING. The clause `and new values 0..m introduced in row
major order' turns the count into a count of equality patterns, and transfer20's triangular
system reduces it to a fixed rational combination of ordinary array counts.

**Here the invariance condition is a real restriction, not a formality.** An `equal edge' is one
whose two cells AGREE, and agreement survives any renaming, so equal-edge conditions reduce.
`Clockwise edge increases' compares cells by SIZE, and a permutation of the alphabet changes the
count, so those entries are refused by the wrapper rather than reduced. That split is why the
298-entry edge family divides the way it does, and every paper of the relabelled family says so.

**A bug the audit caught, and what it was worth.** The wrapper builds one component per alphabet
size and asks the underlying engine for each. A `None' from that engine means EITHER `no
admissible state' OR `refused as too large', and the wrapper treated both as the first —
silently dropping a refused component and leaving a model that undercounts. The audit found it
on A206211, where its smaller cap dropped the largest component.

No paper was affected and the count is unchanged: a dropped component makes the model
disagree with the entry's published DATA, and no hit is recorded without that agreement. But the
guard was wrong, and a wrong guard that happens to be caught downstream is still a wrong guard.
The wrapper now tests the component engine's own size rule before calling it and fails the whole
build when a component would be refused. All 140 papers of both engines were re-audited clean
afterwards.

A LaTeX slip in the same round, caught by the log check that is now routine: the new branch of
the builder emitted `\\[` instead of `\[`, so its display math printed as a line break. Fixed
before anything was delivered.

### 3 Sep 2026: `equal to SOME neighbour' — 56 papers, and a condition that is not local

A statistic of every K X K subblock compared with its neighbours'. Four conditions occur, and
they are not all of the same kind:

| condition | local? | papers |
|---|---|---|
| no neighbouring pair equal | yes | 13 |
| no neighbouring pair differing by more than d | yes | 6 |
| every subblock equal to SOME neighbour | **no** | 29 |
| every subblock equal to exactly one or two neighbours | **no** | 8 |

**The last two are not conditions on a pair, and that is the whole difficulty.** Whether a
subblock has a matching neighbour cannot be decided when its own row is placed: the row BELOW
may yet supply the match. So the state carries, besides the K array rows, a TALLY for each
subblock of the row just completed — one bit for `some', a count capped at three for `exactly
one or two', three being already too many.

A step adds the matches between the two subblock rows to the old row's tallies, requires those
totals to be acceptable (the old row is final at that moment), and starts the new row's tallies
from its own horizontal matches plus the matches just made. A state ACCEPTS when its own tally
is already acceptable — that is what makes the last subblock row, the one with nothing below
it, come out right.

**Both endpoint vectors matter, and getting one wrong is silent.** The first version took the
starting vector as all-ones. That lets the first subblock row count a match with a row above it
that does not exist, and every count came out too large — 12 where the entry publishes 0, for
instance. Only the states whose tally came from their own row may begin an array. The entries
whose first term is 0 (a lone subblock has no neighbour at all, so `equal to some' is
impossible) are the cheapest check that this is right, and they are quoted in those papers.

Statistics covered: trace, determinant, permanent, sum, and diagonal sum less antidiagonal sum,
over 2 X 2 and 3 X 3 subblocks, with horizontal-vertical or diagonal-antidiagonal neighbours,
and the `1/128 the number of' style prefixes divided out. Verified by brute force from the
definition for one entry of each of the four conditions plus four at random. Audit clean, build
logs clean.

### 3 Sep 2026: cell conditions, plain and up to relabelling — 61 papers

The largest remaining cluster of the census is `no element ...' / `every element ...' — about
540 entries in many shapes. Seven of those shapes are now read by one engine, all decided in a
three-row window:

| predicate | papers |
|---|---|
| every cell next to itself plus one and itself minus one (`within the range 0..m') | 19 |
| every cell equal to at least one neighbour | 16 |
| no cell equal to the sum of its neighbours modulo k | 8 |
| no cell adjacent to the value m-x | 3 |
| every cell equal to the NUMBER of its neighbours equal to it | 1 |
| no cell equal to exactly k of its neighbours (up to relabelling) | 13 |
| no cell equal to all its horizontal neighbours or unequal to all its vertical ones (up to relabelling) | 1 |

**Two readings were measured, not assumed.** `within the range 0..m' means each of $v\pm1$ is
required only when it is a letter of the alphabet. And `with no adjacent elements equal' means
adjacent in the SAME named neighbour set — reading it as king-move adjacency gives 0 where the
entry publishes 4.

**The one-row array needed a state of its own.** The natural state is a pair of consecutive
rows, but then the shortest walk describes a TWO-row array, and these entries start at one row.
Allowing the row above to be ABSENT — an extra R states, so S = R(R+1) rather than R^2 — makes
a walk of no steps a one-row array, and its condition is then tested with nothing above and
nothing below, exactly as the entry intends. Every paper of the family states the resulting
first term and notes that testing the boundary the other way (as if the missing rows were
present) would give a different one.

**Relabelling again splits the family.** `plus and minus one', `adjacent to m-x' and `sum
modulo k' all do arithmetic on the letters and do not survive a permutation; `equal to some
neighbour', `equal to exactly k neighbours' and the horizontal/vertical agreement condition do.
The wrapper accepts only the second group.

Verified by brute force from the definition for one entry of each predicate plus three at
random, with the walk-index shift checked explicitly rather than assumed. Audit clean.

**Repeat offence, caught by the log check:** the neighbour offsets were again written as
`$(0,1)$, $(1,0)$` INSIDE a display, the same fault as the 424 papers fixed yesterday. The
check found it before delivery. The lesson is that the fault lives in the habit of writing the
list, not in any one builder, so it will recur until the offset list is produced by one shared
helper; that is worth doing next time a builder needs one.

## 3 Sep 2026 (later) --- occupancy after one move: 43 papers, and a latent bug in the shared determiniser

**The family.** `Number of n X W arrays of occupancy after each element stays put or moves to
some neighbour', with the neighbour set varying (horizontal, vertical, king-move, knight-move)
and optional flags: no occupancy greater than k, every occupancy equal to a or b, no 2-loops.
Each cell holds one unit; every unit independently picks a destination among its allowed
neighbours (or stays); the array recorded is the resulting occupancy count per cell.

**Why it is an image count and not a walk count.** The entry counts DISTINCT occupancy arrays.
Two different assignments of moves can produce the same occupancy array, and they do so
constantly, so no weighting of walks over the movement arrays can give the answer -- the
count is the size of the IMAGE of the movement-to-occupancy map. This is the fourth family
handled by `imagedet.py': the states of the determinised machine are SETS of movement windows
still consistent with the occupancy rows emitted so far, and the count is the number of
distinct output strings, i.e. the number of reachable accepting subsets.

**The bug.** `imagedet.build' added the emitted symbol to the accepting set without testing
whether there was one. A window that cannot legally end an array signals this by returning
`None' from `final', and `None' was being added as if it were an output. The effect is an
extra phantom accepted string: entries publishing 0 came out as 1, entries publishing 4 came
out as 7. It never mattered for the three earlier users of the helper because their `final'
always returns a real row; the occupancy family is the first where a window can be
unfinishable (a unit poised to move off the grid). Fixed, and the earlier family re-verified
unchanged.

**Acting on last round's lesson.** The offset-list display fault was written down last round
as living in the habit rather than in any builder. `texbits.py' now owns that one line
(`offsets_tex'), and the four builders that write neighbour offsets were changed to call it.
The new family was written against the helper from the start and the log check came back
clean on the first compile.

Ten entries covering all seven flag combinations were checked by independent brute force
straight from the definition -- enumerate every assignment of moves, form the occupancy array,
count the distinct ones -- and all ten match. Audit clean.

## 3 Sep 2026 (later still) --- the turn conditions on the occupancy family: 54 papers

The refusal census was redone from scratch after the occupancy round: **2387 non-roster array
entries** carrying a parsable conjectured recurrence that no engine reads, clustered by the
opening of the condition. The largest clusters are

| entries | family |
|---|---|
| ~70 | `avoiding patterns X and Y` |
| ~70 | `of occupancy after each element ...` (the rest of the occupancy family) |
| ~70 | `every consecutive three elements in ...` |
| ~64 | `no element x(i,j) adjacent to ...` |
| ~53 | `every K X K subblock ...` |
| ~53 | `nondecreasing x(i,j)+x(i,j-1) in the i ...` |

The second was taken this round: 62 of the 70 are the occupancy family again, with a condition
that ties the direction a token LEAVES a cell to the direction in which another token ARRIVES
there. Four wordings appear, and all four are conditions on an ordered pair `(d, d')' of
offsets, where a token moves by `d' onto a cell whose own token moves by `d'':

  `without consecutive moves in the same direction'          d' = d
  `without move-in move-out straight through or left turns'  d' = d or d' left of d
  `without move-in move-out left turns'                      d' left of d
  `without 2-loops or left turns'                            d' = -d or d' left of d

**What `left' means was not guessed.** Three readings are possible for a neighbour set with
diagonal offsets --- a 45-degree turn, a 90-degree turn, or any turn through an angle strictly
between 0 and pi --- and they give different counts. Brute force from the definition on
A221604 (`horizontal or antidiagonal', where a 90-degree test would never fire at all)
separates them: 2, 10, 54, 287 for `any left turn', against 2, 20, 192, 1840 and 2, 24, 270,
3024 for the two fixed angles. The published data is 2, 10, 54, 287. The chirality is fixed by
the same check: `any RIGHT turn' gives 2, 6, 32, 172.

**Transposition reverses a turn.** Half the family is written `W X n' and the walk runs down
the transpose, which is a reflection; the left-hand test has to be negated in that frame, not
merely applied there. A221610 is the check that it is: the model reproduces 0, 2, 10, 53, 269,
1378 and brute force on the untransposed grid agrees.

**A token that stays put makes no turn.** For the `stays put or moves' entries a zero offset
on either side of the pair carries no condition; reading it as a `straight through' would
forbid standing still, and the first terms alone rule that out.

The window is unchanged from the plain occupancy engine: every offset moves the row index by
at most one, so a pair whose first move is made in row i has its second move in row i-1, i or
i+1, and one window of three consecutive move-rows decides both the occupancy row and every
forbidden pair sourced in the middle row. Each ordered pair is tested exactly once, from the
row of the token making the first move.

Verified by brute force straight from the definition --- enumerate every assignment of offsets,
discard those containing a forbidden pair, form the occupancy array, count the distinct arrays
--- for **one entry of each of the 16 combinations** of (condition, orientation, stays-put,
occupancy cap) that occur among the 54. All 16 match. The forbidden-pair test in the check is
written out separately from the engine's, so the two do not share a reading of the wording.
Audit clean, no LaTeX errors.

**Still open in this cluster:** 8 entries of the shape `(n+k) X 1 arrays of occupancy after
each element moves up to +-k places', a one-column form with long-range moves. Not attempted
yet; the state is a window of k move-rows and the shape is a different parse, not a different
idea.

## 3 Sep 2026 (fourth round) --- consecutive triples along four directions: 51 papers

The next cluster off the refusal census. The names read

    Number of (n+2)X(W+2) 0..m arrays with every consecutive three elements in every row and
    column having exactly two distinct values, and in every diagonal and antidiagonal not
    having exactly two distinct values, and new values 0 upwards introduced in row major order.

with the four directions carrying independent conditions on how many DISTINCT values a triple
may hold: `exactly two', `not exactly two', `one or two', `two or three', or a direction left
unconstrained. Eleven distinct combinations occur among the entries settled.

**Two uses of the same symmetry.** Every clause counts distinct values, so nothing compares
letters by size and the condition is invariant under permuting the alphabet. That is what lets
the `new values 0 upwards' clause be handled by the falling-factorial inversion, as in the
earlier relabelling families. It is ALSO what makes the walk affordable. A state is a pair of
consecutive rows --- every triple lies in three consecutive rows --- and there are up to
`i^(2W)' of them, which is `5^18' for the widest entries and unreachable. But the transfer
matrix commutes with the action of `S_i' on the alphabet and the end vector is invariant, so
`M^t tau' is constant on orbits and the walk may be run on ORBITS of pairs, that is, on the
equality PATTERN of the pair. The orbit of a pattern showing `p' letters has `i(i-1)...(i-p+1)'
members, so the start vector is a falling factorial and the end vector is all ones. That is a
factor of up to `i!' and it is the whole difference between reachable and not: A252688 comes
out at 135 states where the unlumped pair space is 4^6 = 4096 per component.

**Reach, measured.** 130 names read; 59 carry no parsable conjectured recurrence; 51 settled;
19 remain over the state cap even at 120000 states, and one exhausted the annihilation budget.
The wall is the fixed dimension: entries with fixed side 3, 4 or 5 come in comfortably, side 6
and 7 sometimes, sides 8 and 9 over alphabets of 4 or 5 letters do not. That is a recorded
wall, not an unexplored idea --- the orbit count itself is what exceeds the cap, and there is
no further symmetry in the problem to quotient by.

Verified by brute force straight from the definition --- fill the cells in row major order,
allow a cell to introduce a new letter only when every smaller one is present, reject as soon
as a completed triple fails --- for **one entry of each of the 11 condition combinations**,
five terms each. All 11 match. The check uses neither the transfer matrix, nor the orbit
reduction, nor the falling-factorial inversion. Audit clean, no LaTeX errors.

**A rendering fault caught before delivery, not after.** The per-direction table was first
written with its prose column inside math mode, which collapsed `a row' to `arow' and turned
the en-dash of `nw--se' into two minus signs. The log check does not catch this --- it is
valid TeX --- so it was caught by extracting the text of a built PDF and reading it. That
extraction is now part of the routine for any paper carrying a table.

## 3 Sep 2026 (fifth round) --- monotone statistics of short runs: 161 papers

The largest single family so far. Two shapes, both from the same idea: take a statistic of a
short run of cells, form the array of its values, and require that array to be monotone.

    Number of (n+1)X(K+1) 0..m arrays with nondecreasing f(x(i,j),x(i,j-1)) in the i direction
    and nondecreasing g(x(i,j),x(i-1,j)) in the j direction.

    Number of (n+k-1)X(K+k-1) 0..m arrays with nondecreasing <statistic> of every k
    consecutive values in every row and column.

In the first, `f' runs across a horizontal pair and its array must not decrease DOWN a column,
while `g' runs down a vertical pair and its array must not decrease ALONG a row --- the two
directions are crossed, which is the only subtle part of the reading. `f' and `g' range over
sum, difference, absolute difference, min and max in eleven of the twenty-five combinations.
In the second, one statistic --- sum, maximum, minimum, median, or maximum minus minimum ---
serves the rows and the columns alike, over runs of two or three.

**The window.** In the first shape every comparison names four cells lying in two consecutive
rows, so a single row is a state and the whole model is the `(m+1)^W' rows with an edge for
each admissible pair: 9, 16, 27 states for the common sizes. In the second, a row comparison
lives inside one row but a column comparison relates the runs starting at rows `i' and `i+1'
and so spans `k+1' rows; the state is the window of the last `k' rows, and a walk of no steps
is an array of exactly `k' rows.

**Nothing here is invariant under renaming.** Every statistic either does arithmetic on the
letters or compares them by size, so the pattern reduction that carried the previous family is
not available and is not attempted; the walk runs over the alphabet the entry names. That is
worth writing down because the two families sit next to each other in the census and look
alike from the outside.

**Reach, measured.** 361 names read; 178 carry no parsable conjectured recurrence; 161
settled; 4 remain over the state cap at 60000 states, all of them wide arrays over the larger
alphabets.

Verified by brute force straight from the definition --- fill the cells in row major order and
test each comparison the moment both of its runs are complete, in the orientation the name
itself writes --- for **one entry of each of the 17 statistic combinations**, four terms each.
All 17 match.

**A bug of my own, caught by the sweep rather than by a paper.** The first run reported 143
`terms failed' and no proofs. The cause was in the new engine's parse output, not in its
mathematics: the pair-interface in `uniform' divides every term by `p["frac"]', and the new
parser did not set that key, so every call raised. Nothing false was produced --- the failure
was total and loud --- but it is a reminder that the interface contract is a real part of an
engine and not boilerplate. Fixed, the same sweep proved 143 immediately.

## 3 Sep 2026 (sixth round) --- clashing pairs and the row-major precedence clause: 43 papers

    Number of n X W 0..m arrays with no element x(i,j) adjacent to [itself or] value m-x(i,j)
    <directions>, top left element zero, and 1 appearing before 2 3 and 4, and 2 appearing
    before 3 in row major order.

The condition proper is local --- two cells neighbouring in one of the named directions may
not carry values summing to `m' (nor equal values, when the entry says `itself or') --- so one
array row is enough state. What is new is the tail. `top left element zero' fixes one cell and
so restricts which rows may begin the array. The precedence clause is the interesting one: it
asks that, reading the cells in ROW MAJOR order, certain values make their first appearance
before certain others. Several of these entries gloss themselves as counting `unlabelled
6-colorings'.

**The clause needs one bit per named value and nothing more.** A precedence `u before v' is
decided at the moment `v' is first written, so carrying the SET of named values already written
is enough: a cell may introduce `v' only when every `u' required to precede it is in the set.
The state is then a pair (array row, set), and the set has at most `2^6' values in the largest
case. That is the whole trick, and it works only because an `n X W' walk visits the cells in
exactly row major order.

**Where it stops, and why.** For a `W X n' entry the walk runs across the columns and does NOT
visit the cells in row major order --- a value's first appearance in row major order can be
lowered by a later column --- so the set is not enough and the state would have to carry, for
each named value, the smallest row it has yet appeared in together with the order among ties.
Those **14 entries are refused**, deliberately, rather than modelled wrongly. A further 7 are
over the state cap: `W' of 6 or 7 over alphabets of 6 or 8 letters puts the row count alone
past a million.

**A bug caught by the first comparison against data.** The direction offsets are transposed for
a `W X n' entry, and transposing `(1,-1)' gives `(-1,1)'. The pair test only looked at offsets
with a positive row step, so `(-1,1)' was being read as the diagonal `(1,1)' --- the
antidiagonal condition was silently dropped and the diagonal one imposed twice. A232922 came
out 27, 96, 432 where the entry publishes 27, 54, 246. The clash relation is symmetric, so the
fix is to normalise every offset to a nonnegative row step before use.

Verified by brute force straight from the definition --- fill the cells in row major order in
the orientation the name itself writes, test each clause as soon as it can be tested --- for
**one entry of each of the 15 combinations** of directions, self-clash, top-left clause,
precedence clause and orientation. All 15 match. Audit clean, no LaTeX errors.

**One thing deliberately not claimed.** The papers do not assert that the two tail clauses pick
exactly one array out of each renaming class; that is the entry's own gloss and it is quoted as
such. The model and the independent check both test the clause exactly as written, so nothing
rests on the gloss being right.

## 3 Sep 2026 (seventh round) --- pattern avoidance in rows, columns and diagonals: 111 papers

    Number of (n+2) X W binary arrays avoiding patterns 001 and 100 in rows and columns.
    Number of n X W 0..m arrays avoiding the pattern z-1 z-1 z in any row, column or
      nw-to-se diagonal.
    Number of n X 2 0..3 arrays avoiding 11 horizontally, 22 vertically, 33 antidiagonally
      and 00 diagonally.

One family, three ways of writing it. A pattern is either ABSOLUTE, a literal word like `001',
or RELATIVE, written with a free letter as in `z-1 z-1 z' or `z z+1 z', which forbids every
window standing in those differences whatever `z' is. Each entry attaches one or more patterns
to one or more of the four directions, and the entries differ in whether the patterns are
shared by all directions or named per direction.

Nothing is longer than three letters and no direction moves the row index by more than one, so
every occurrence lies inside three consecutive rows: the state is the window of the last `L-1'
rows, `L' the longest pattern. The window starts all-absent, so a walk of no steps is the EMPTY
array --- which matters, because several of these entries have offset 0 and publish `a(0)=1'.
Starting the walk at one-row arrays instead would have lost those entries silently at the
shift-matching step.

**Three parsing faults, all found by the first comparison against data, none reaching a paper.**

  1. `nw-to-se' was being read as `ne-to-sw'. The window is indexed from its LAST row, so the
     earlier cells of an occurrence step BACK along the direction; the code stepped forward,
     which reverses the diagonal. A202428 gave 6, 36, 114 against the published 108, 390.

  2. `antidiagonals?' placed before `antidiagonally' in the alternation matched only the stem
     and left a stray `ly' for the next clause, so every per-direction entry naming
     `antidiagonally' was refused. The longer word has to come first.

  3. The filler words `in any' after a pattern list needed stripping repeatedly, not once, so
     `... z z+1 z in any row, column ...' was refused.

**Reach, measured.** 409 names read; 89 carry no parsable conjectured recurrence; 3 are already
settled on the entry and were skipped; 111 proved; none left over the cap.

Verified by brute force straight from the definition --- fill the cells one at a time in the
orientation the name itself writes, reject as soon as a completed run matches a forbidden
pattern --- for **one entry of each of the 32 pattern/direction/orientation combinations**.
All 32 match. Audit clean, no LaTeX errors.

**A note on engine ordering.** This engine was added at the END of the engine list rather than
the front. The list is tried in order and the first engine that reads a name claims it, so a
new engine placed first can silently take a name another engine already models correctly. These
names come from the refusal census --- by construction no earlier engine reads them --- so the
position is free here, but the safe end is the end.

## 3 Sep 2026 (eighth round) --- two more clusters: 47 + 34 papers

**`containing all values 0..m' --- one row of the same inverse, not the sum of its rows.**

    Number of (n+1) X W 0..m arrays CONTAINING ALL VALUES 0..m with every 2 X 2 subblock
    having one or two distinct values, and new values 0..m introduced in row major order.

These sit right next to the relabelling families already done and look identical from outside.
The difference is three words. Writing `N_j' for the admissible patterns on exactly `j' letters
and `L_i' for the admissible arrays over `i' letters, `L = F N' with `F' the falling-factorial
triangle. The neighbouring families count `N_1 + ... + N_K' and use the weights `1^T F^{-1}'.
This one must use every letter, so it counts `N_K' alone and uses the single row
`e_K^T F^{-1}' of the SAME inverse. Nothing else changes: the subblock condition counts
distinct values, so it survives renaming, and each `L_i' is a walk on the rows.

The initial zeros in these entries are the sharp test of that clause --- a small array cannot
show `K' letters at all --- and the brute force reproduces them.

**47 papers**; all 47 names of the cluster parsed, 30 of the 77 read carry no parsable
recurrence, none over the cap.

**`each element equal to the number of its neighbors that ...' --- self-referential, and the
end vector is not all ones.**

    Number of n X W integer arrays with each element equal to the number of horizontal and
    antidiagonal neighbors less than itself.

Every entry counts its own neighbours of a stated kind: zero, equal to a fixed value, smaller,
smaller or equal, unequal, equal, exactly one smaller, or differing by exactly one. The array
is self-referential but only locally --- a cell's neighbours lie in three consecutive rows ---
so the state is (row above, current row) and a step settles the middle row of the window it
completes.

Two boundaries had to be got right and both were tested against data rather than assumed.

  * The entry says `integer arrays' and names no alphabet, but one is forced: an entry is a
    count of neighbours in the named directions, of which there are two per direction, so every
    entry lies in `0..2d'. That is a bound, not a guess.

  * The condition for the LAST row is settled with nothing below it, so it belongs to the END
    vector, which is therefore not all ones: a row that counts correctly only when something is
    written below it must not finish an array. And the walk starts at the EMPTY window, so a
    walk of no steps is the empty array --- A197049 publishes `a(0)=1' and without that state
    the model began 2, 4, 10 against the published 1, 2, 4, 10.

**34 papers**; 43 names in the cluster, all parsed, 8 carry no parsable recurrence, 2 remain
over the state cap at 300000 states (width 6 and 7 over a five-letter alphabet), and **one was
correctly refused as already settled**: A197049 carries a link to Spahn's proof of its
generating function, and the openness check caught it before any work was spent. That is the
check doing its job, and it is worth recording that it fires.

Verified by brute force straight from the definition for **one entry of each of the 11 subblock
combinations and each of the 21 neighbour/predicate combinations**. All 32 match. Audit clean,
no LaTeX errors.

## 3 Sep 2026 (ninth round) --- rows and columns as base-b numbers: 72 papers

    Number of (n+2) X (W+2) 0..1 arrays with each row and column divisible by 7, read as a
    binary number with top and left being the most significant bits.

A row is a base-`b' number of `W' digits, left digit most significant; a column is a base-`b'
number of as many digits as the array has ROWS, top digit most significant. The entry asks for
divisibility, or non-divisibility, by given moduli, with the row and column moduli sometimes
different, and a few entries add that the rows and the columns are each in lexicographic order.

**Why this is not a local condition, and why it is still a walk.** A column's value depends on
every row of the array, so no window of rows decides it. Its RESIDUE, however, is built one row
at a time by Horner's rule: adding a row at the bottom shifts every earlier digit one place up
in significance, so `v <- b*v + x' and reduction commutes with that. The vector of `W' column
residues is therefore a bounded state, the row condition is imposed as each row is chosen, and
the column condition is read off the END vector --- which is accordingly not the all-ones
vector. The lexicographic clause needs two more things in the state: the previous row, to
compare rows, and one bit per adjacent column pair recording whether that pair has been equal
in every row so far, because a column comparison is settled by the first row where the two
differ.

**A flaw in my own cap handling, caught by the audit and not by the sweep.** The build had a
cheap up-front size guard `e^W > 8*cap`, meant to refuse a hopeless model before doing work.
But nothing ever enumerates the `e^W` residue vectors --- they are reached lazily --- so the
guard was measuring the wrong quantity. Six entries proved at a large cap were then REFUSED by
the audit, which re-builds at `cap = S+1`: their reachable state count `S` is far below `e^W`,
so the guard tripped. The models were right; the guard was wrong. It now measures the one thing
that is genuinely enumerated up front, the `b^W` candidate rows. All 72 models rebuild
identically at `cap = S+1` and the audit is clean.

That is worth keeping in mind generally: a size guard has to bound what the code actually
enumerates, or it will refuse work it could do and --- worse --- make the audit disagree with
the sweep for a reason that has nothing to do with the mathematics.

**Reach, measured.** 218 names read; 137 carry no parsable conjectured recurrence; 2 are
already settled on the entry and were skipped; 72 proved; none left over the cap.

Verified by brute force straight from the definition --- enumerate every array of the size the
name states, turn each row and each column into a base-`b' number, test the divisibility and
the lexicographic order directly --- for **one entry of each of the 11 combinations** of
row/column modulus, negation, base, lexicographic clause and orientation. All 11 match.

## 3 Sep 2026 (tenth round) --- sums along rays: 72 papers

    Number of n X W 0..3 arrays with no element equal to zero plus the sum of elements to its
    left or one plus the sum of elements above it or one plus the sum of the elements
    diagonally to its northwest or one plus the sum of the elements antidiagonally to its
    northeast, modulo 4.

A cell is forbidden to equal, modulo `m', a constant plus the sum of everything lying before it
along a ray: west, north, northwest, northeast. The sums are unbounded and none of them is
local; their RESIDUES are, because each is built one term at a time. Taking the array one slice
at a time along the side that grows, and indexing positions of a slice by `p':

    the ray running along the slice  is the running total as the slice is filled
    the opposite ray                 U'[p]  = U[p]  + x[p]
    the northwest ray                NW'[p] = NW[p-1] + x[p-1],  NW'[0] = 0
    the northeast ray                NE'[p] = NE[p+1] + x[p+1],  NE'[W-1] = 0

Advancing one slice moves a cell one step along each ray, and the term picked up is exactly the
cell just left behind; the diagonal rays also shift one position, right for northwest and left
for northeast, which is what the index shift says.

**Where it stops, and this is a real boundary rather than a size limit.** For an `n X W' entry
every ray points into slices already written. For a `W X n' entry the slice is a COLUMN and the
northeast ray points into columns still to come: no state built this way can hold it, and
reversing the walk only moves the problem to the west ray. Those **15 entries are refused**,
deliberately. Transposing does not help either --- transposition carries northeast to
southwest, which is equally unwritten.

**Reach, measured.** Of the 91 names in the cluster, 18 are refused (the 15 above and 3 whose
wording carries something else besides the ray clauses); 115 names read in all; 42 carry no
parsable conjectured recurrence; one is already settled on the entry; 72 proved; none over the
state cap.

Verified by brute force straight from the definition --- fill the cells one at a time in the
orientation the name itself writes and, for each candidate value, walk each ray to the edge of
the array and add the entries up --- for **one entry of each of the 7 ray-set/modulus/
orientation combinations**. All 7 match. Audit clean, no LaTeX errors.

## 3 Sep 2026 (eleventh round) --- each cell must SEE the next value modulo m: 50 papers

    Number of n X W 0..3 arrays x(i,j) with each element horizontally or vertically next to at
    least one element with value (x(i,j)+1) mod 4 and at least one element with value
    (x(i,j)-1) mod 4, no adjacent elements equal, and upper left element zero.

Every cell has to SEE, among its neighbours in the named directions, at least a stated number
carrying the value one more than its own modulo `m', and in most of the family at least a
stated number carrying the value one less. Some entries forbid equal neighbours as well, and
all of them fix the top left cell at zero.

The window is three consecutive rows, as for the self-counting family, and the same two
boundaries decide the answer:

  * the rows that may BEGIN an array are those whose first entry is zero --- the top-left
    clause is a restriction on the start vector, not a separate condition;
  * the condition for the LAST row is settled with nothing below it, so it belongs to the END
    vector, which is therefore not all ones. A row that sees enough neighbours only because a
    further row is written below it must not finish an array.

The leading zeros these entries publish are the sharp test of the second point --- a small
array has too few neighbours for any cell to see what is demanded --- and the model reproduces
them.

**Reach, measured.** 70 names read; 14 carry no parsable conjectured recurrence; 50 proved.
**Seven names of the cluster are refused by the parser and are worth naming**: they read
`Number of black-square subarrays of ...' or `white-square subarrays of ...'. They are not
attempted here rather than being forced into this model.
**[Corrected 4 Sep 2026.** This section originally called those seven "an image count over a
different object", and that was wrong; see the 4 September entry. The conditions are stated in
diagonal and antidiagonal neighbours only, which never change the colour of a cell, so the two
colour classes are independent and one of them is just a rotated grid. All of them, and the
same wording elsewhere, are now proved by `transfer69`.]

Verified by brute force straight from the definition for **one entry of each of the 22
direction/count/modulus/equality/orientation combinations**. All 22 match. Audit clean, no
LaTeX errors.

**A note on the square symmetric matrices, checked again and still a wall.** The largest
untouched cluster in the census is now the `(n+1) X (n+1) -2..2 symmetric matrices with every
2 X 2 subblock having sum zero and k distinct values' family, about 60 entries. Both sides grow
with `n', so adding a row also adds a column, and symmetry ties the two together; the state
would have to be the whole new row, whose length grows. That is the same wall recorded for the
square families in August and it has not moved.
**[Corrected 4 Sep 2026. It has now moved, and the reasoning above was the wrong reasoning: it
asked whether a WALK ON ROWS could work and answered no, without asking whether the condition
itself could be solved. `2 X 2` sum zero is linear, and solving it makes the matrix a function
of its own diagonal --- one sequence, not a growing row. All 60 are proved; see the 4 September
entry.]**

## 3 Sep 2026 (twelfth round) --- two clusters: 30 + 39 papers

**Offsets forbidden to repeat, counted up to renaming.**

    Number of 3 X n 0..2 arrays with no element equal to any value at offset (-2,-2) (-1,0)
    or (-1,1) and new values introduced in order 0..2.

The clause reads `in order 0..2', NOT `in row major order', and that difference turned out not
to matter --- for a reason worth writing down rather than guessing around. The condition tests
only whether two cells are EQUAL, so it survives renaming; the admissible arrays therefore fall
into classes, and in any fixed reading order each class contains exactly one array whose
distinct values appear first in the order 0,1,2,.... So the entry counts CLASSES whatever
reading is meant, the ambiguity is empty, and the ordinary falling-factorial inversion gives
the count from the counts over alphabets of each size. That is stated as a lemma in every paper
of the family.

The second observation is that equality is symmetric, so an offset and its negative forbid
exactly the same pairs. Replacing each offset by whichever of the two points BACKWARDS along
the growing side makes every pair tested once, from the later of its two cells, and the state
is then a window of the last two slices. Without that step the offsets `(-1,1)' in a `W X n'
entry would reach into columns not yet written.

**30 papers**; all 30 names of the cluster parse, none over the cap.

**Repeated values along a row and down a column.**

    Number of n X W 0..m arrays with every repeated value in every row and column greater than
    the previous repeated value.

A REPEATED VALUE is an entry equal to the entry just before it in the scan; each row and each
column produces a sequence of them, and consecutive members must stand in a stated relation ---
unequal, equal, greater, greater or equal, one larger modulo k, not one larger. The first
repeated value of a scan is unconstrained.

The reading was pinned against the data before anything was built. A267729 (`n X 2', binary,
`greater than or equal') publishes 4, 16, 64, 225, 784: perfect squares, so the two columns are
independent and the row condition never bites at width 2. The single-column counts are
2, 4, 8, 15, 28: at length 4 exactly one binary word fails, and it is `1100' --- a repeat of 1
followed later by a repeat of 0. That is the reading, and no other candidate produces a single
failure there.

One scan runs inside a slice and is settled as the slice is written; the other runs across
slices and needs, per position, the previous slice's entry (to see a repeat) plus the last
repeated value so far. Entries whose relation is built from equality carry the renaming clause
and go through the falling-factorial inversion; entries whose relation compares letters by size
or does arithmetic on them carry no such clause --- they could not --- and are counted over
their own alphabet. The two cases are kept apart by the parser rather than by hand.

**39 papers**; all 43 names of the cluster parse, 9 carry no parsable recurrence, one exhausted
the annihilation budget even at four times the usual limit and is left unclaimed.

**A parsing fault, caught by the refusal count and not by any answer.** Nine names put the
phrase `the previous repeated value' TWICE --- once per clause --- and the body of the name was
being matched non-greedily, so it stopped at the first occurrence and the rest of the name went
unrecognised. The names were refused, not mis-read, so nothing false could have come out; but
nine entries would have been silently lost. Matching to the LAST occurrence and stripping the
phrase from each clause fixes it.

Verified by brute force straight from the definition for **one entry of each of the 9 offset
combinations and each of the 21 relation/renaming/orientation combinations**. All 30 match.
Audit clean, no LaTeX errors.

## 3 Sep 2026 (thirteenth round) --- forbidden runs: 33 papers

    Number of (n+2) X W 0..2 arrays with no increasing sequence of length 3 horizontally or
    antidiagonally downwards.
    Number of n X W 0..m arrays with no occurrence of three equal elements in a row
    horizontally, vertically or nw-to-se diagonally, and new values 0..m introduced in row
    major order.

Two conditions of one shape: a run of three consecutive cells taken along a direction of the
grid is forbidden when its entries are strictly INCREASING, or when they are all EQUAL. Every
run lies inside three consecutive rows, so the state is the window of the last two, with a row
not yet written carried as a symbol.

The equal-run family closes with a renaming clause and the increasing-run family does not ---
and could not. `All equal' is a statement about equality and survives any permutation of the
alphabet, so those entries go through the falling-factorial inversion; `strictly increasing'
compares letters by size and does not. The parser keeps the two apart and refuses an increasing
run carrying a renaming clause outright; none occurs in the data.

**A real bug, and the reason it matters more here than in the neighbouring engines.** Half these
entries are written `W X n' and the walk runs down the transpose. Every earlier engine of this
kind normalises a direction to point downwards, negating it when necessary, because the
conditions there were symmetric --- equality does not care which end of a pair you start from.
Here it does: transposing carries an antidiagonal read from the northeast to one read from the
southwest, and an INCREASING run read backwards is a DECREASING run. The first version
normalised the sense away and six entries came out wrong from the first term --- 1, 27, 729
against a published 16928, 388908, 8946936. The fix is to carry a `reversed' flag with each
direction and test the run in the sense it is actually read. The papers say so explicitly,
because a reader checking the transposed entries would otherwise have to rediscover it.

Nothing false was published: the mismatch was caught by the routine comparison against the
entry's own terms, before any paper existed.

**Reach, measured.** 158 names read; 110 carry no parsable conjectured recurrence; 33 proved;
3 remain over the state cap at 300000 states and 3 exhausted the annihilation budget even at
three times the usual limit.

Verified by brute force straight from the definition --- fill the cells in row major order in
the orientation the name itself writes, reject as soon as a completed run is equal or
increasing --- for **one entry of each of the 13 kind/length/direction/renaming/orientation
combinations**. All 13 match. Audit clean, no LaTeX errors.

**Delivery note.** The file uploads were rate-limited (HTTP 429) for the whole of the previous
round and the start of this one, so the zip set could not be sent. The papers are in the repo
either way; the zips are re-packed on every round and the next successful send carries the
current set.

## 3 Sep 2026 (fourteenth round) --- the lines of a K X K window: 60 papers

    Number of (n+2) X W 0..3 arrays with every 3 X 3 subblock row and column sum 3 or 6 and
    every diagonal and antidiagonal sum not 3 or 6.
    Number of (n+2) X W 0..3 arrays with no row, column, diagonal or antidiagonal in any
    3 X 3 subblock summing to 0 2 4 5 7 or 9.
    Number of (n+3) X W 0..1 arrays with no 4 X 4 subblock diagonal sum less than the
    antidiagonal sum.

One engine, five ways of writing the same kind of condition on the eight lines of a `K x K'
window --- its `K' rows, its `K' columns, its main diagonal, its antidiagonal:

    a list of forbidden sums for all four kinds of line at once;
    a required list for the rows and columns and a forbidden list for the two diagonals,
      or the other way round;
    a forbidden value named separately for each kind of line;
    one line's sum COMPARED with another's (`diagonal sum less than the antidiagonal sum',
      `central row sum equal to the central column sum');
    the sum of the whole window;
    and one variant asking every line sum to be PRIME.

A window lies in `K' consecutive array rows, so the state is the window of the last `K-1' rows
and a step settles every window the new row completes. The comparison forms need nothing extra:
both lines being compared live in the same window.

**A case that had to be handled rather than refused.** Some entries are narrower than the
window --- `(n+2) X 3' with a `4 X 4' subblock --- and then no window fits inside the array at
all. The condition is vacuous, not unsatisfiable, and the entry counts every array of its
shape. The first version returned an empty model for those and lost them; the fix is simply to
let the window loop run over an empty range and say so. Ten entries came back.

**An interface bug, caught by the sweep.** The new engine returns a four-part model
`(adj, start, end, S)' and was registered in the five-part list by mistake, so every term
computation divided by a denominator that did not exist and 47 entries failed at once. The
failure was total and loud, nothing false came out, and the fix was one line --- but it is the
second time this session that an engine's INTERFACE, not its mathematics, cost a sweep. The
list an engine belongs to is part of writing the engine.

**Reach, measured.** 155 names read; 61 carry no parsable conjectured recurrence; 60 proved;
one remains over the state cap at 300000 states. Of the 265 names in the wider `subblock ...
sum' cluster, 171 are refused: most are the `(n+K) X (n+K) symmetric matrices' whose two sides
both grow --- the wall recorded in August and re-checked twice since, **and lifted on 4 Sep
2026 by solving the sum-zero condition instead of walking the rows** --- and the rest state
conditions of a different shape (`ne-sw antidiagonal difference unequal to its neighbors',
`each element being the sum mod k of two others') that this engine does not read.

Verified by brute force straight from the definition --- fill the cells in row major order in
the orientation the name itself writes, test a window as soon as its last cell is placed ---
for **one entry of each of the 20 rule/window/orientation combinations**. All 20 match. Audit
clean, no LaTeX errors.

## 3 Sep 2026 (fifteenth round) --- neighbours counted, predecessors read: 41 papers

    Number of n X W binary arrays with each 1 adjacent to exactly two other 1s.
    Number of n X W 0..2 arrays with every 1 immediately preceded by 0 to the left or above,
    no 0 immediately preceded by a 0, and every 2 immediately preceded by 0 1 to the left or
    above.

Two kinds of clause, one engine. An ADJACENCY clause counts, for every cell carrying a stated
value, how many of its four neighbours carry another stated value; some entries split that into
so many vertically and so many horizontally. A PRECEDENCE clause looks backwards: the
predecessors of a cell are the cell to its left and the cell above it.

**Four readings, all pinned against the published terms before anything was built.** These
names are terse and each one had a plausible alternative.

  * `every 1 immediately preceded by 0 to the left or above' means at least one EXISTING
    predecessor carries 0 --- so a 1 in the top left corner, which has no predecessor at all,
    is forbidden. Reading it as `whichever predecessors exist are 0' gives 5, 27, 147 and
    reading it as `both, where they exist' gives 5, 17, 63, against a published 3, 20, 102.
  * `preceded by 0 0' means the two cells to the LEFT read 0,0 in order, or the two ABOVE do.
  * `preceded by both a 1 and a 0' means the two predecessors show one of each.
  * `adjacent' means the four rook-step neighbours, not the eight king-move ones: for the
    first entry the king reading gives 1, 9, 18, 30 against a published 1, 3, 6, 10, and for
    another it gives 1, 7, 4, 5 against 1, 7, 10, 23. Two independent entries agree on the
    same reading, which is what makes it a reading rather than a fit.

The two kinds of clause meet in one state, the pair (row above, current row), but they are
settled at different moments. A precedence clause reads only backwards, so it is settled as its
