own row is appended. An adjacency clause for a row needs the row BELOW it, so it is settled one
step later and the LAST row of an array is settled by the end vector --- which is accordingly
all ones for a precedence-only entry and not all ones for an entry with an adjacency clause.
The papers say which case they are in.

**Reach, measured.** 46 names read, all 42 of the cluster parse; 4 carry no parsable
conjectured recurrence, one is already settled on the entry, 41 proved, none over the cap.

Verified by brute force straight from the definition for **one entry of each of the 9
clause combinations**. All 9 match. Audit clean, no LaTeX errors.

## 3 Sep 2026 (sixteenth round) --- a local family and a global one: 38 + 40 papers

**`every 0 next to a 1 and every 1 next to a 2'.** Each of a short list of pairs asks that every
cell carrying the first value have at least one neighbour carrying the second, in the named
directions; some entries add that no two neighbours are equal. Three consecutive rows decide
one, and --- as in the other `must see a neighbour' families --- the LAST row is settled by the
end vector, which is therefore not the all-ones vector. 38 papers; 39 names in the cluster, all
parse, 5 carry no parsable recurrence, one is over the state cap.

**`some element plus some horizontally or vertically adjacent neighbor totalling two no more
than once'.** This one is worth writing down properly, because it is the first GLOBAL condition
in a while.

    over the whole array, the number of PAIRS of adjacent cells whose entries add up to T
    must be at most one, or exactly one.

No window of the array decides that: the count runs over everything. What saves it is that the
condition can only distinguish `none', `one' and `two or more', so the count may be carried
CAPPED at two and is then a bounded state. Every adjacent pair lies inside one row or across two
consecutive rows, so appending a row adds exactly the pairs inside it and the pairs joining it
to the row above; the state is (previous row, capped count) and the end vector accepts the
states whose count is what the entry asks. 40 papers.

The pairs are unordered --- a pair of CELLS, counted once and not once from each end. That is
checked, not assumed: the binary 2 X 2 case has 16 arrays, and 5 of them have two or more
adjacent pairs summing to 2 (the four with three ones, the one with four), leaving 11, which is
the published second term. Counting ordered pairs would double every count and give a different
threshold.

**Refused and named:** the same cluster contains entries reading `Number of 2X2X2 triangular
0..n arrays with some element plus some adjacent element totalling n exactly once'. Those are a
different object twice over --- a triangular array, and an ALPHABET that grows with `n' rather
than a shape that does. They are not attempted here.

Verified by brute force straight from the definition for **one entry of each of the 13
combinations in each family**. All 26 match. Audit clean, no LaTeX errors.

## 3 Sep 2026 (seventeenth round) --- pair sums and the order put on them: 40 papers

    Number of (n+1) X W 0..m arrays with column and row pair sums b(i,j)=a(i,j)+a(i,j-1) and
    c(i,j)=a(i,j)+a(i-1,j) <condition>.

Two derived arrays: `b' adds each cell to its LEFT neighbour, `c' adds each cell to the one
ABOVE it. Three conditions occur, and they need three different amounts of state.

  1. `nondecreasing in column and row directions, respectively' --- `b' must not decrease down
     a column and `c' must not decrease along a row. The two directions are CROSSED: `b' is
     built across a row and tested down a column, `c' the other way about. Each comparison names
     four cells of `a' lying in two consecutive rows, so a single row is the state.

  2. `such that b(i,j)*b(i-1,j) - c(i,j)*c(i,j-1) is nonzero' --- all four terms are built from
     rows `i-1' and `i', so again a single row is the state. Worth writing down because the
     expression looks as if it reaches further than it does.

  3. `such that rows of b and columns of c are lexicographically nondecreasing' --- the ROW
     comparison is again two consecutive rows, since a row of `b' is built from one row of `a'.
     The COLUMN comparison is not local: which of two columns of `c' is smaller is settled by
     the first row in which they differ. The state carries one bit per adjacent column pair
     saying whether that pair has been equal in every row so far, the same device as in the
     digit-divisibility family.

**A note on the first form.** Its mathematics is the same as the monotone-statistic family
already done --- the horizontal statistic tested down a column, the vertical one along a row ---
but the entries WRITE it completely differently, naming `b' and `c' explicitly instead of
saying `nondecreasing x(i,j)+x(i,j-1) in the i direction'. Nothing in the earlier engine reads
this wording, and rather than widen a published engine's parser these are handled fresh. The
cost is a second engine for one idea; the benefit is that no already-delivered paper is touched.

**Reach, measured.** 92 names read; 47 carry no parsable conjectured recurrence; 40 proved; one
remains over the state cap at 300000 states.

Verified by brute force straight from the definition --- form both derived arrays in full and
test the condition on them --- for **one entry of each of the 15 form/order/alphabet
combinations**. All 15 match. Audit clean, no LaTeX errors.

## 3 Sep 2026 (eighteenth round) --- two wordings of families already built: 10 + 13 papers

A short round, and the honest description of it is that both engines are READERS, not new
mathematics. The census keeps producing clusters whose condition is one already modelled and
whose WORDING no existing parser reaches.

**Distances instead of offsets.** `no element equal to another within two positions in the same
row or column', `within a city block distance of two', `at a city block distance of exactly
two', each with the renaming clause. These name a set of offsets by a distance rule rather than
listing it, and once the rule is read out the condition is the offset family exactly: no cell
may equal the cell at any offset of the set, counted up to renaming. The module reads the three
phrasings and hands the offsets to the offset engine's build; the papers say so, and print the
offset list the rule names.

**The modulus in front instead of at the end.** `no element equal to the sum modulo 3 of
elements to its left or elements above it' is the ray-sum condition with the modulus written
first and the words `the sum of' dropped from every clause after the first; a clause with no
constant carries the constant zero. Same walk, same residues carried slice by slice.

**Reach, measured.** 31 names read for the distance form, 19 for the ray-sum form. 10 and 13
proved. Nine of the distance entries are out of reach --- five over the state cap and four
whose annihilation test did not finish even at four times the usual budget --- and one ray-sum
entry is refused because it names the NORTHEAST ray in a `W X n' array, which points into
columns not yet written; that is the same wall recorded when the ray-sum engine was written.

**On reusing an engine rather than widening one.** Both modules delegate their build to the
engine that already does the work. That is deliberate: widening a published engine's parser
risks changing what it reads for a name already papered, and the audit would then disagree with
the sweep for a reason that has nothing to do with the mathematics. A new reader over a shared
build costs one small file and touches nothing already delivered.

Verified by brute force straight from the definition for **one entry of each of the 7 distance
combinations and each of the 5 ray combinations**. All 12 match. Audit clean, no LaTeX errors.

### 3 September 2026 — the clockwise perimeter of a 2 X 2 subblock: 90 papers

R. H. Hardin states a whole family of conditions on the four corners of a `2 X 2` subblock read
round its perimeter. Writing the block as `p q / r s`, the clockwise cycle is
`p -> q -> s -> r -> p` and the counterclockwise one runs the other way; `cw(B)` and `ccw(B)`
count the steps at which the value rises. Every undirected edge is walked once by each cycle in
opposite directions, so `cw + ccw = 4 - (equal edges)`.

Fourteen distinct wordings, one engine (`transfer64`):

* the corners read clockwise spell one of a listed set of binary words;
* `cw = ccw`, or `cw <= ccw`, in every subblock, with or without "no adjacent elements equal";
* the steps round the block rise by at most one in one of the two directions — or in exactly one;
* every block strictly increasing one way with a single decrease, optionally plus "at least two
  adjacent blocks having the same increasing direction";
* one or four distinct clockwise edge differences;
* the same `cw` throughout the whole array;
* `cw` nondecreasing rightwards and downwards, optionally with `ccw` nonincreasing;
* `cw(B)` equal to — or never equal to — `ccw` of the left and upper neighbours;
* `cw` matched across horizontal neighbours and `ccw` across vertical ones, or never matched.

Every reading was pinned against published data before any engine was written, not guessed.
Two mattered. "Clockwise pattern 0000 0011 or 0101" does NOT fix the starting corner: with the
start fixed there are 3 two-by-two binary arrays, up to rotation there are 7, and 7 is what the
entry publishes. (Direction is not ambiguous here — every binary necklace of length 4 is its own
mirror image, so reading a `2 X 2` block clockwise or counterclockwise gives the same set of
patterns.) "Strictly increasing clockwise or counterclockwise with one decrease" means three
rises and one fall with no equal ends, i.e. `cw` in `{1,3}`; that gives 240 arrays of shape
`2 X 4` over `0..4`, which is 20 times the 12 the entry publishes.

Most of the conditions are settled by two consecutive rows. Three are not, and each needed its
own carrier in the state: the neighbour comparisons look at the subblock ABOVE, so the state
keeps one small number per column for the row pair just closed; "the same `cw` throughout" is a
single value in `{0,1,2,3,4}`, unset until the first subblock fixes it; and "at least two
adjacent blocks having the same increasing direction" is an existential, so it is one bit, set
when first witnessed and never cleared, with the end vector reading it.

Rows are grown column by column with pruning rather than tried whole. The strict conditions
accept so few rows that enumerating all `m^W` candidates per state would have been the entire
cost of the build; with pruning the widest case, `(n+1) X 7` over `0..4`, builds in seconds.

90 entries proved. 91 of the 94 in the census reproduce their published data; the three left are
two `T(n,k)` tables with a free column index and one `(n+1) X (n+1)` square array, all correctly
refused — the width has to be a fixed number for the row walk to have a bounded state. One of
the 91 turned out not to be open.

All 90 pass the independent brute force: every array of the entry's own width with two and with
three rows, written out cell by cell and tested by the entry's own words, with no window, no
state and no recurrence involved. `audit_uni.py` rebuilds all 90 at `cap = S+1` and finds the
claim holding for 40 further terms with the threshold tight in every case.

### 3 September 2026 — lexicographic order on a derived 2 X 2 array: 68 papers

A second Hardin family, unrelated to the first: every `2 X 2` subblock is reduced to ONE number
and the resulting `(R-1) X (W-1)` derived array `D` is required to have its rows and its columns
in lexicographic order. Ten statistics appear, and one engine (`transfer65`) reads them all:
the determinant `ps-qr`, the permanent `ps+qr` (with or without "and all 2 X 2 permanents
nonzero"), the sum `p+q+r+s`, the sum of squares, and the order statistics `v4-v1`, `v4+v1`,
`v2+v3`, `(v1+v4)-(v2+v3)`, `v3-v2`, `v3-v1` on the four values sorted.

Both axes and both senses occur — "nondecreasing rowwise and columnwise", "nondecreasing
columnwise and nonincreasing rowwise", "nondecreasing rowwise and nonincreasing columnwise" —
and each was checked against published data before the engine was written. "Rowwise" compares
consecutive ROWS of `D` as whole words, not entries along a row; that reading, and the mixed
senses, reproduce the first two terms of every wording exactly.

The row comparison is local: a row of `D` comes from two array rows, so comparing consecutive
rows of `D` reads three array rows and nothing more. The column comparison is NOT local — which
of two columns is smaller is decided by the first derived row in which they differ, and that row
can be arbitrarily far down. What is bounded is what is still OUTSTANDING: one bit per adjacent
pair of columns, saying whether that pair has agreed in every derived row so far. While the bit
is set the pair is undecided and the next derived row must not break the order; once cleared the
pair is settled and nothing further is asked of it. (`transfer61` uses the same device on a
different derived array; the two families share no wording and no parser.)

Every statistic in the list is unchanged when a `2 X 2` block is transposed, so the one entry
written with `n` as the number of columns is the same problem with the two axes exchanged.

68 entries proved, all reproducing published data, all clean under `audit_uni.py` at `cap = S+1`
with tight thresholds, and all 68 checked against an independent brute force that writes out
every two- and three-row array cell by cell, forms the derived array and compares its rows and
columns as whole words.

**Not taken, and why.** The neighbouring wording "rows and columns lexicographically
nondecreasing" applies the same order to the ARRAY itself, but every entry that carries it also
carries a global sum condition — "zero-sum", or "column sums nondecreasing". A running total
over a growing array is not a bounded state, and neither is the difference between two column
sums: adjacent columns of a lexicographically ordered binary array can have sums that differ by
as much as the number of rows. Those ~18 entries are a wall for the row-walk method, not pending
work. The three entries adding "the instance counts of every value within one of each other" are
out for the same reason.

### 3 September 2026 — rolling polyhedra and graph colourings of an array: 66 papers

A family that had never been touched, and the cleanest in the roster. Fix a finite graph `G`.
An array is a map from its cells to the vertices of `G`, and the condition is that any two cells
adjacent in one of the named directions (horizontal, vertical, diagonal, antidiagonal) carry
vertices joined by an edge of `G`. Some entries also fix the top-left cell at vertex `0`.
Hardin's titles call these "rolling cube footprints" and "rolling icosahedron footprints": a die
rolled over the array leaves the face that touched each cell, and consecutive cells must show
faces that share a cube edge.

Six graphs, one engine (`transfer66`):

* `0..5 label faces of a cube` — two faces adjacent unless opposite: the octahedron graph
  `K(2,2,2)`, 4-regular on 6;
* `0..7 label vertices of a cube` — `Q3`, 3-regular on 8;
* `0..19 label faces of an icosahedron` — two faces adjacent when they share an edge: the
  dodecahedron graph, 3-regular on 20;
* `0..11 label vertices of an icosahedron` — the icosahedron graph, 5-regular on 12;
* `0..20 label nodes of the fully triangulated graph` — a triangle of side 6 in the triangular
  lattice, 21 nodes and 45 edges;
* `label nodes of a graph with edges 0,1 0,3 ...` — the edge list written out in the entry.

The labelling never has to be guessed, and the papers say why: the condition mentions only the
edge relation, so a relabelling is a bijection between the arrays of two labellings; and the
four named graphs are vertex-transitive, so even "starting with 0" is the same count whichever
vertex is called `0`. Every graph and every direction set was checked against the first two
published terms before the engine was written — for instance 64 = 4^3 one-row arrays of width 4
on the octahedron graph, and 6912 for two rows.

The state is a single slice and nothing more: every named offset joins cells in one slice or in
two consecutive ones. Slices are grown a cell at a time with pruning, which is what keeps the
list short — a slice of length 7 over 20 vertices is one of 1.28e9 words, but only a few
thousand are legal.

66 entries proved. 13 more parse and are correct but exceed the build cap: they are the widest
transposed shapes, where the slice added at each step is a column of the ORIGINAL array and the
entry's direction list does not include the one that would constrain it — so no pruning applies
and the state list is the full `N^W`. That is a size wall on this encoding, not a gap in the
reading; all 13 are reproduced correctly by the brute force.

All 66 pass the independent brute force, and the graphs there are built by a DIFFERENT route
from the engine's — the cube from its corner points and face normals in space, the icosahedron
as a pentagonal antiprism capped at both poles — so a wrong graph would have shown up as a
mismatch rather than being confirmed twice by the same mistake. `audit_uni.py` rebuilds all 66
at `cap = S+1`, clean, thresholds tight.

### 4 September 2026 — lumping the rolling-polyhedron walk by the graph's symmetry: 10 papers

Yesterday's graph-colouring engine left 13 entries refused for size: the slice alphabet was too
large to carry one state per slice, up to 3.2 million legal slices. Ten of them are now proved,
by running the walk on ORBITS of slices instead.

The condition names only the edge relation of `G`, so every automorphism of `G` acts on the
arrays, and acting on slices it commutes with the transfer matrix while fixing the all-ones end
vector. That is exactly the hypothesis for lumping: `M^m·1` is constant on each orbit, so the
quotient matrix `M̂(O,O') = #{v in O' : v may follow the representative of O}` runs the same
walk, with the orbit sizes as starting weights. `|Aut|` is 48 for both cube graphs and 120 for
both icosahedron graphs, and that is the factor the state count comes down by — for one entry
3,200,000 slices become 26,800 orbits.

The entries that fix the top-left cell at 0 are handled by a second consequence of the same
symmetry, which also removes the awkward non-invariant start vector. All four graphs are
vertex-transitive, so for any two vertices there is an automorphism carrying one to the other,
and applying it cellwise is a bijection between the arrays starting at one vertex and those
starting at the other. The fibres of `x(0,0)` are therefore equal, and the entry's count is the
unrestricted count divided by the number of vertices. So the lumped walk is run with no start
condition at all and divided once at the end.

Orbit representatives are generated directly, never by listing slices and grouping them — that
listing is the thing being avoided. A slice is built one cell at a time carrying the set of
automorphisms that have so far written the same prefix, and abandoned as soon as one of them
would write a smaller letter. What reaches the last cell is the lexicographically least member
of its orbit, exactly one per orbit, and the set still tied there is its stabiliser, so the orbit
size falls out of the same walk by orbit-stabiliser.

`transfer66` was NOT widened to do this. Instead it now decides, from an exact count of its own
slices and edges by a dynamic programme over the columns — a function of the entry alone, not of
any cap a caller passes — whether the plain construction is affordable, and declines when it is
not. `transfer67` takes exactly what `transfer66` declines. The 66 papers already published are
untouched: all 66 still parse to `transfer66`, and `audit_uni.py` reproduces every one.

Verified: all 10 reproduce their published data; all 10 pass the independent brute force, which
applies the "starting at 0" condition DIRECTLY and so tests the divide-by-`N` argument as well;
the computed automorphism groups were checked to be groups (closed under composition and
inverses, every element a bijection preserving the edge set); `audit_uni.py` clean at
`cap = S+1` with tight thresholds.

Three of the 13 remain out: two dodecahedron-graph entries of width 6, where even the orbit
count is about 533,000, and one cube-face entry of width 7 whose lumped edge count still exceeds
12 million. A further reduction would need a different encoding, not a bigger cap.

### 4 September 2026 — what a cell asks of the cells around it: 56 papers

Seven Hardin wordings, one engine (`transfer68`), all of them a statement made by one cell about
the cells at a fixed set of offsets — horizontal `(0,±1)`, vertical `(±1,0)`, diagonal
`(±1,±1)`, antidiagonal `(±1,∓1)`, the eight knight offsets, or a single named direction
("vertically above" `(-1,0)`, "horizontally left" `(0,-1)`, "diagonally above and left"
`(-1,-1)`):

* `x` is not the average of the neighbours it has (13 entries, two direction lists);
* `x` is not the average of its horizontal and vertical neighbours (5);
* `x` together with its neighbours does not average to a stated value (3);
* `x` is not equal to a strict majority of its neighbours (4, one of them knight-move);
* no strict majority of the neighbours is `x+1 mod 3` — the "rock, paper and scissors drawn
  positions" (14);
* `x` is not equal BOTH to the cell above and to the cell to its left (8);
* `x` is the sum mod `m` of one named group of neighbours, or of another (11).

Only offsets landing inside the array count, so a border cell simply has fewer neighbours, and a
cell with none satisfies an "is not the average of" condition vacuously. That reading is what the
published first terms say, and every one of the seven was checked against three terms before the
engine was written.

The mechanism is the general one for conditions that reach BOTH ways. A cell's condition reaches
`U` rows up and `D` rows down, so a row is settled by a window of `U+D+1` consecutive rows; the
state is the last `U+D` of them and each step settles exactly one row. When `D > 0` the last `D`
rows of a finished array have never been tested, so the end vector is not all ones: a state is
accepted exactly when those rows pass with nothing below them, tested by running the same rule on
the window with absent rows appended. Knight-move offsets reach two rows each way, so that entry
uses a five-row window.

56 entries proved. All 56 pass the independent brute force — every array of the entry's own width
with a few rows written out cell by cell, each cell tested against the neighbours it has, no
window and no end vector involved. `audit_uni.py` rebuilds all 56 at `cap = S+1`, clean, with
tight thresholds.

**Not taken.** Fifteen entries of the same wording are `white square subarrays of ...` or
`black-square subarrays of ...`, left to the known black/white-square wall.
**[Corrected the same day: that wall was a misreading, and all fifteen are now proved by
`transfer69` — see the next entry.]** One more,
`lower triangles of a 3 X 3 0..n array`, has the alphabet growing with `n`.

### 4 September 2026 — the black/white-square wall was not a wall: 21 papers

**A recorded dead end that was wrong.** The ledger has carried "black/white-square subarray
entries (7)" as a measured wall since the early rounds, and yesterday's round widened it to 15
with the reasoning that these count IMAGES of arrays under projection onto one colour class of
the chessboard, which a walk count does not do. That reasoning was mistaken, and the pool is now
21 papers.

Look at what the conditions actually say. Every entry in the pool states its condition purely in
terms of DIAGONAL and ANTIDIAGONAL neighbours. A diagonal step changes `i` and `j` each by one,
so it changes `i+j` by 0 or ±2 and never changes the parity. Every neighbour of a white cell is
white. The condition therefore splits into two systems sharing no cell, one per colour, and the
entry states its clauses about the class it names — which its "upper left element zero" settles
outright: for a black subarray that clause fixes the cell `(0,1)`, not `(0,0)`, and the data
agrees to the term. So there is no projection and no image-counting anywhere in it; there is a
condition on one sublattice, and the sublattice is a grid again, rotated 45 degrees.

The engine (`transfer69`) walks the original array a row at a time. The class cells of a row sit
at every other column, and the two shapes alternate with the row parity, so the state records
which shape the next row has. All four offsets move exactly one row, so a row is settled by three
consecutive rows and the state is the last two; the condition looks one row down as well as up,
so the last row of a finished array is untested when the walk stops and the end vector is the
indicator of the states whose last row passes with nothing below it.

Two conditions and two extra clauses, all pinned against published data first:

* no cell equal to a strict majority of its diagonal and antidiagonal neighbours (14);
* every cell diagonally next to one with value `x+1 mod 4`, and no neighbour equal to it (7);
* "upper left element zero" — the first cell of the SUBARRAY in reading order;
* "values `0..m` introduced in row major order" — carried as one more number in the state, how
  many distinct values have been introduced so far; a cell may take any value already used or the
  next one up, and the count updates along a row, so a value first used early in a row makes a
  larger value legal later in the same row. (Getting that wrong — capping the whole row by the
  count at its start — was the one bug in this round; it was loud, the model missed the data by
  a factor of two on every term, and nothing false could come of it.)

21 entries proved, all reproducing published data, all clean under `audit_uni.py` at `cap = S+1`
with tight thresholds. The independent brute force lists the colour class from `i+j` directly and
backtracks over assignments to it, with no rows, no window and no state; it was re-run from an
empty done-file after being rewritten, so no result rests on the earlier version.

**The lesson for the ledger.** A wall recorded as "this family counts something a walk cannot
count" is worth re-reading whenever the family is revisited: the barrier here was a
misdescription of the object, not a measurement. Walls established by SIZE (state counts,
alphabets that grow with n) are measurements and have all held.

### 4 September 2026 — the square symmetric matrices: 60 papers, and the biggest wall gone

**The second recorded dead end to fall in a day, and for the same kind of reason.** The ledger
has carried the `(n+K) X (n+K) -m..m symmetric matrices with every 2 X 2 subblock having sum
zero and k distinct values` family — about 60 entries, the largest untouched cluster in the
census — as a wall since August, re-checked three times. Every check asked the same question:
can a walk on rows work when both sides grow? No, it cannot. But that was never the only
question. **The condition itself can be solved.**

`2 X 2` sum zero is linear. Put `y(i,j) = (-1)^(i+j) x(i,j)`; the four entries of a subblock
then alternate in sign, so their sum is the mixed second difference of `y`, and it vanishes
everywhere exactly when `y(i,j) = f(i) + g(j)`. Symmetry forces `f - g` constant, and absorbing
half of it into each side gives

    x(i,j) = (-1)^(i+j) (u_i + u_j) / 2 .

Setting `j = i` gives `u_i = x(i,i)`: **the sequence is the diagonal of the matrix**, so this is
a bijection, not merely a parametrisation. The range clause `-m..m` on every entry reduces to
`|u_i| <= m`, and the entries all being integers forces the `u_i` to share a parity. A
two-dimensional family in which both sides grow is a one-dimensional family of sequences.

What is left is not local, though. The four entries of the subblock at `(i,j)` are built from
the consecutive pair `(u_i, u_{i+1})` and the consecutive pair `(u_j, u_{j+1})` — for ALL `i`
and `j`, not just adjacent ones — so the number of distinct entries must be right for every
ORDERED PAIR of consecutive pairs anywhere in the sequence. The consecutive pairs used must form
a clique in a fixed graph on at most `(2m+1)^2` vertices.

Carrying the set of pairs used is exponential and dies at once (measured: over 400,000 states
for half the direction sets, and unbounded for the rest). Carrying what that set FORBIDS does
not: the pairs still available are the intersection of the neighbourhoods of the pairs already
used, and intersections of neighbourhoods are few. With the state `(last value, that
intersection)` every one of the nine distinct-value clauses builds in under a second, the
largest at `S = 586`.

60 entries proved, every one reproducing its published data. Verified: an independent brute
force writes symmetric matrices out entry by entry over the entry's own range and tests each
`2 X 2` subblock by the entry's own words, with no sequence, no sign pattern, no clique and no
state; and Lemma 1 itself is checked separately, by counting symmetric sum-zero matrices
directly and counting admissible sequences, for every size up to 5 and range up to `-4..4`.
`audit_uni.py` clean at `cap = S+1`, thresholds tight.

**The lesson, sharpened.** Yesterday's was: a wall recorded as "this counts a different kind of
object" is a misdescription and deserves re-reading. Today's is narrower and worse: a wall
recorded as a SIZE measurement can still be wrong, if what was measured was the size of one
particular encoding. "Both sides grow, so the state is unbounded" measures the row walk. It says
nothing about whether the object admits a different description. Three re-checks all repeated the
same measurement and never asked the other question.

### 4 September 2026 — what a cell demands of SOME neighbour: 62 papers

The counterpart to this morning's `transfer68`, which read what a cell says about ALL its
neighbours. Here the statements are existential, and seven of them share one engine
(`transfer71`):

* every nonzero cell has a neighbour at least as large as itself (15 entries, offsets named
  outright as "NW, E or S" — the set `(-1,-1), (0,1), (1,0)`, which transposing carries to
  itself);
* every cell has a neighbour at least as large AND one at most as large (15);
* every cell has neighbours equal to each of two named values (9, two of them adding "2
  introduced before 3 in row major order");
* every cell of one named value has a neighbour of another (26, including king-move);
* every cell of one value has an allowed NUMBER of neighbours of another (3);
* every cell equals at least one of its neighbours (4);
* every cell sees its own value plus one and minus one among its neighbours, sometimes with no
  neighbour equal to it (13).

All seven readings pinned against three published terms first. Same window mechanism as
`transfer68`: `U` rows up, `D` down, state the last `U+D`, end vector the indicator of the states
whose remaining rows pass with nothing below.

**A parser trap worth recording.** These entries write the directions as ADVERBS — "neighboring
horizontally or vertically", "horizontally, diagonally or antidiagonally" — where the earlier
families wrote adjectives ("its horizontal and vertical neighbors"). The direction regex was
`\b(horizontal|vertical|...)\b`, and `\b` fails inside "horizontally": the word boundary is not
there. Half the family silently refused to parse. A refusal is invisible — it looks exactly like
"there was nothing there" — which is why the coverage count is checked against the census every
round rather than trusted.

**And a cap-dependent guard, the recurring one.** The first version guarded on
`A^(W*K) > 8*cap`. `audit_uni.py` rebuilds at `cap = S+1`, and one entry with `S = 1478` but
`3^12 = 531441` rows in principle was refused on rebuild — the model was right, the guard was a
function of the caller's cap. Fixed to an absolute bound on the rows actually enumerated, with
the state count still held down by the `len(order) > cap` test. All 62 now rebuild to exactly
the same `S`. This is the fifth time a cap-dependent guard has done this; the rule is: **a guard
must be a function of the entry, never of the caller's cap.**

62 entries proved, all reproducing published data, all checked against an independent cell-by-cell
brute force, `audit_uni.py` clean at `cap = S+1` with tight thresholds.

### 5 September 2026 — a number read off a subblock, compared with the subblock next door: 32 papers

`transfer72`. The block is `2 X 2` (six entries also `3 X 3` at the same time), and it is
reduced to a single number by its two diagonals: the northeast entry minus the southwest, the
northwest plus the southeast, `max(diagonal) - min(antidiagonal)`, `max - max`, `max + min`, or
`sum - sum`. The condition is that this number is UNEQUAL to the same number at a neighbouring
block, in the directions the entry names.

Two readings had to be pinned before anything was built, and both were pinned against published
terms:

* a "neighbour" block is the block ONE STEP OVER, overlapping the first — not the next disjoint
  block. `A253307` gives 518, and only the overlapping reading produces it;
* a comparison is imposed only when BOTH blocks lie inside the array. A block near an edge is
  simply compared in fewer directions.

The window is `K+1` rows for the largest block size `K`, since a block and the block one row
lower span `K+1` rows and nothing reaches further. State: the last `K` rows. End vector: all
ones, and this time genuinely so — a block whose neighbour would sit below the last row is not
compared in that direction at all, because that neighbour is not part of the array. Confirmed by
rebuilding all 32 models and counting zeros in the end vector: none.

**Two bugs, both found by the brute force and both of the silent kind.** The first: `win_ok`
only tested blocks starting at window row 0, so horizontal comparisons in the final rows were
never tested and short arrays were untested altogether. Fixed by testing every offset inside the
window — a comparison then gets tested several times as the window slides, which costs nothing
and is what makes the "every comparison is tested" argument airtight. The second: a column index
of `-1` was not rejected, so Python wrapped it to the last column and over-restricted the
two-column entries (`A253307` came out 364 against a published 518). The bounds test in
`blockstat` now rejects `j < 0` as well as `j + k > W`. Both are reminders that an index test
must reject the negative side explicitly in a language where negative indices are legal.

32 entries proved, all reproducing published data, all checked against an independent
reading-order backtracking brute force run from an empty done-file, `audit_uni.py` clean at
`cap = S+1` with tight thresholds.

### The silent-refusal audit (5 September 2026)

Every census entry's condition skeleton was compared against the skeletons of entries already
papered, to find conditions a sibling of which is already proved but which no engine reads. 164
exact skeleton matches. Broken down by the engine that proved the sibling: **95 `gf-implies-rec`**
— which is a per-entry method, not a parser, so those are not refusals at all — then
commuting-subblock 19, clashing-pair 12, transfer-matrix 10, cell-condition 6, closedform 4,
cell-condition-pattern 4, common-sum 3, monotone-subblock 3, the rest one or two each. By shape:
82 same-orientation, 32 stated as `T(n,k)` tables (the conjecture is made "for every column", so
it needs an argument uniform in `k`, not one model), 30 transposed, 12 square, 7 other head, 1
with no `n`. The transposed and same-orientation ones are the ones worth a parser widening; the
`T(n,k)` ones are a different piece of work.

### 6 September 2026 — the full re-check, and five papers withdrawn

The whole roster was re-checked against a fresh OEIS export (the 6 Sep 2026 dump, pulled for
this pass; the working copy had been eleven days old). What was done, and what it found:

**Still open.** The settlement scan ran over all 8665 A-numbers on the new export: 27 hits, every

verified and used for computations. - _Fung Lam_", which reads as a numerical check.

* `audit_deep.py`, a replacement for `audit_all.py`, rebuilds each array model from the entry's

* Every conjecture quoted in a paper was re-evaluated on the entry's current data: 5185 testable,

* `regf.py` was re-run from scratch on the symbolic papers. The ones in its scope came back

Still not re-verified in this pass and recorded as such: 70 models too large to rebuild inside a

**Double counting.** 29 entries hold two papers. Comparing the conjecture each paper quotes shows

* `A124431` — Mathar posted the SAME recurrence twice, in 2012 and 2016. Two papers, one theorem.

* `A306948` — one conjecture on the entry, two papers. **One withdrawn.**

That is the failure this project is most exposed to, and nothing was checking for it: `rank.py`

Roster 8697 → 8692.

### 6 September 2026, second pass — the settlement scan had holes: four more withdrawn

The first pass of the re-check ran the settlement scan as written and found three dead papers.
Then the closed-form audit — rebuilding each `walk-closed-form` model and evaluating the entry's
own polynomial past every published term — flagged `A188555`, and the reason was not the
mathematics. The entry carries this, from Feb 2024:

> The number of such words satisfy the recurrence given below and, hence, the empirical/
> conjectured formulas become true. — *Miquel A. Fiol*

The scan's copula list was `is|are|was|were`. **"become true" is a settlement and did not match.**
So the pattern was widened and, because a widened regex is still a regex, a deliberately
OVER-broad sweep was run behind it: any line mentioning a conjecture together with any word that
could belong to a settlement, read by hand. Thirteen entries, of which three more were real:

* `A081672` — "E.g.f. satisfies y''' − … = 0, which **implies Mathar's conjectured recurrence**."
  — *Robert Israel*, Jun 2016.
* `A166587` — "G.f. G(x) satisfies …, **from which follows** … **as well as Mathar's conjecture**."
  — *Robert Israel*, May 2016.
* `A309878` — "**All conjectures stated above hold true.** See links." — *Sela Fried*, Jul 2024.

All four withdrawn. Roster 8692 → 8688.

**The lesson.** The settlement scan is the gate the whole count rests on, and it was being trusted
as a filter when it is only a search. Three of these four were found not by the scan but by a
MATHEMATICAL audit that had no interest in settlement wording at all — the closed-form check —
and by the over-broad sweep run afterwards. A regex over English cannot be complete; what makes it
safe is running something behind it that does not depend on wording. Both are now part of the
re-check.

**The recovery papers, the riskiest class, are clean.** The 111 papers that reconstruct a
recurrence the entry does not write down (it names only the order, with the recurrence in a linked
file) rest on one step: the model's MINIMAL recurrence has exactly the stated order, so any
recurrence of that order is that one. Rebuilding all 111 and recomputing the minimal order with
Berlekamp–Massey confirms it in every case — 68 sequences and 43 tables, the last three columns
too large for exact arithmetic and pinned modulo two primes instead.

One trap on the way: the minimal order came out one too big everywhere. The model counts the
empty array and the short ones the entry never publishes, and each unpublished leading term raises
the minimal order by one. The order to compare is the one the tails settle to, and once that is
used, every case matches. A check that disagrees with 40 papers at once, by exactly one, is the
check that is wrong.

Verification status of the roster after both passes: 7387 array models rebuilt and checked, 372
recurrences matched against the entry's data, 207 generating-function proofs re-derived, 157
closed forms checked against the model, 111 recovered recurrences confirmed, 21 read by hand;
341 symbolic papers whose route the re-derivation script does not cover and 70 models too large to
rebuild in a container turn are recorded as NOT re-checked, and the comment drafts for those carry
a hold.

### 6 September 2026, third pass — the array side is fully re-checked, and `uniform.py` was hiding two engines

Every array paper in the roster has now been rebuilt and re-checked. Getting there turned up two
silent gaps in `uniform.py`, the single interface every sweep goes through.

**`transfer7` could not be built through `uniform` at all.** `uniform.build` dispatches on a list
of engines whose `build` takes a `cap`; `transfer7.build` takes only `p`. It fell through to the
generic call, which passes `cap=`, raising `TypeError` — swallowed by the `except Exception:
return None` that guards the dispatch. So every `transfer7` entry came back "too big" from a model
that builds in five seconds. Forty-two of the seventy models the audit could not rebuild were
this one bug. `transfer3` and `transfer6` have the same signature and were handled specially;
`transfer7` was simply missed. Fixed, with its own branch in `build`, `size`, `terms` and
`threshold`.

**`uniform` does not know `transfer7`'s LUMPED model, or its second reading.** The sweep that
produced the relabelling papers calls `build_lumped`, whose states are row PATTERNS rather than
rows — which is why a model `uniform` reports as 4.8 million states is 430 in the paper — and it
falls back to `parse_nb` when `parse_name` refuses. `uniform` does neither. The audit now uses the
sweep's own path for that family; nineteen more models came back in four minutes.

**The last one, `A222142`, needed a different idea.** 15625 rows, and the matrix has 244 million
entries, which is more than a container turn. But the condition is per adjacent PAIR of cells, so
the vertical part of the transfer matrix is a sixfold tensor power of one 5×5 matrix and the
horizontal part is a mask on rows. A vector goes through a step in six passes of a 5×5
contraction — about half a million operations instead of 244 million — and the counts and the
recurrence come out exactly. Recorded here because the trick generalises: **whenever the condition
is a product over columns, the transfer matrix never has to be written down.**

Also re-checked in this pass: all 188 table papers, column by column (315 columns, no failures),
and all 157 empirical closed forms, evaluated against the rebuilt model past every published term.

Verification standing: **8535 of 8688 re-checked this round**, with zero mathematical failures
found. The 153 not re-checked are the symbolic papers whose route the re-derivation script does
not cover — bespoke number theory, hypergeometric closed forms, Ore-algebra divisions,
coefficient extractions — and their comment drafts carry a hold.

The last 153 were the ones no engine rebuilds and no parser reads: bespoke number theory,

Each was checked by computing what it says.

* **37 congruence and periodicity papers** — "a(n) mod k is eventually periodic with period

  congruent to 1 mod 8" — tested on the published terms.
* **11 identity papers** — a(n) equals a bisection, a difference, a multiple of ANOTHER entry:
  read both entries and compare.
* **73 more** by reading the entry from scratch and evaluating every conjectured statement on it,
  rather than only the line the paper quotes. That mattered: for a paper whose known side is a
  closed form the entry states as fact, the quoted line is not the conjecture at all, which is
  why the earlier audit skipped 42 of these.
* **27 bespoke results** computed directly: Detlefs' primorial characterisation and his two
  Fibonacci–Fermat ones (219781 confirmed as the smallest composite passing both), Bala's strong
  divisibility, parity and three gcd-product valuations, the Euler-number periodicity

  binomial transform, Seidov's representation count, Lallouet, Detlefs–Wolstenholme, Mathar's

**Three false alarms, all mine, and all the same cause.** The bespoke checks were written from
the PDFs, and `pdfminer` drops superscripts. `k^n` came out as `kn`, so Bala's strong divisibility
conjecture was checked in a form the paper's own first paragraph says is false. `A129364` was
checked with the division the wrong way round. `A047926` was checked without the off-by-one the
paper explicitly corrects. Every one of the three looked like a dead paper for a few minutes.
**Read the claim from the ENTRY, which is plain text, not from the paper's rendered PDF.**

**Roster status: all 8661 A-numbers re-checked, no mathematical failure found anywhere.** Five
papers were withdrawn in the first two passes for being already settled or already counted, and
three attributions were corrected. What the re-check did NOT find is as much the point as what it
did: after four passes over 8688 papers, the errors were five dead results, three wrong names, and

`oeis-comments.json` / `.txt` now carry a draft for 8636 papers. 41 have none: their build

### 6 September 2026, fifth pass — one stripped word cost 269 candidates: 13 proofs

The re-check left one loose end: `A251331` ("every 2 X 2 subblock summing to 2, 4, or 6") is a
name no parser reads, and it had to be rebuilt by hand. That is a silent refusal, so the question
is how wide it goes.

`transfer57` reads the subblock line-sum family. Its patterns spell the allowed sums as
`[\d\s]*\d` — digits and spaces — because the entries it was written against wrote "3 6". Many
write "3, 6" or "1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, or 7", and those never matched. Widening the class was one
edit. The second was worse and would have hidden the first: the parser strips the word "or" from
the body before matching, which also removes the one inside the literal
`no row, column, diagonal or antidiagonal`, so **the pattern could not match its own text** once
an entry wrote "or" anywhere. Both fixed; the literal now tolerates the missing word.

Census after the fix: **269 entries** of this family that no engine had ever read. Sweeping them:

* **13 proved**, all reproducing their published data, all confirmed by an independent brute
  force written from the entry's words (the last one, `A251994`, by writing out all 16.7 million
  three-row arrays with no model at all — the shared brute force prunes cell by cell and does not
  finish it inside a turn);
* 22 more state the recurrence only as an order, in a linked file — the recovery route, not yet
  attempted;
* the rest are over the state cap, carry no recurrence, or are already settled.

A regression pass rebuilt all 60 existing papers of the family through the widened parser and
checked them against their data: unchanged.

**The lesson is the one from 4 September, sharper.** That day an adverb (`horizontally` vs
`horizontal`) hid half a family. This time it was a word the parser removed itself. Both are
invisible: a refusal looks exactly like "there was nothing there". The census against the corpus
is the only thing that finds them, and it now runs after every parser change, not only after a
new engine.

### 6 September 2026, sixth pass — a family that is not an array count at all: 46 proofs

The coverage census, re-run after the parser fix, has 706 non-roster array entries no engine
reads. Its biggest cluster is not an array count: **76 entries counting PERMUTATIONS of the cells
of a fixed-width array**, in which every cell moves by one of a short list of offsets —
"Number of n X 2 array permutations with each element moving zero or one space diagonally,
horizontally or vertically". Three were papered; 53 carry a conjectured recurrence.

That count is a **permanent**, and for a fixed width it is a walk count. Number the cells in
row-major order; an offset moves a cell by between `lo` and `hi` places in that order; process
the cells in order and let each choose its image. Once the cell at position `k` is done, position
`k+lo` can never be chosen again, so it must already be taken, and nothing beyond `k+hi` can be
taken yet. **The state is which of those `hi-lo+1` positions are taken, and nothing else.**

The two boundaries turn out to be one condition. Images above the first row do not exist, so the
walk starts with exactly the window positions above the array marked taken; images below the last
row do not exist either, so the walk must END with exactly those marked and nothing beyond. In
the window's own coordinates the two masks are equal — **the start state is also the only
accepting state**.

**The reading, pinned first as always, and it was not the obvious one.** "moving zero or one space
diagonally, horizontally or vertically" is NOT the eight king moves: each word names an AXIS, two
opposite offsets, and "antidiagonally" is a separate word for the other diagonal. Reading it as
king moves gives 24 where `A189305` publishes 14. A search over offset subsets found the seven
that reproduce the entry, and the same reading then reproduced 30 of the 32 entries testable by
hand. The two it missed say "right-handed knight moves (out 2, right 1)" — four of the eight
knight offsets, two out and one to the right of that heading, pinned the same way.

46 proved, every one reproducing its published data, all 46 confirmed by an independent brute
force that matches cells to images over the whole grid with no window and no mask, and
`audit_uni.py` clean at 2842 of 2842.

The `n X n` members of the family are correctly refused: both sides grow, so there is no fixed
width to walk along. That is a real wall, not a parser gap.

**Worth carrying forward:** the census clusters by the WORDS of the condition, and the biggest
cluster was a different kind of object hiding in an array-shaped name. Looking only for new
conditions on arrays would never have found it.

### 6 September 2026, seventh pass — the median condition: 15 proofs

Next cluster down the census: 32 entries reading "with the minimum plus the maximum equal to the
lower median plus the upper median in every 2 X 2 subblock", half of them with "unequal".

It looks like four separate order statistics and is one line: sort the block's four entries as
`a <= b <= c <= d`, and the minimum plus the maximum is `a+d` while the two medians are `b` and
`c`. The condition is `a+d = b+c`. Nothing depends on where in the block each value sits — it is
a statement about the multiset, symmetric under rearranging the block and under adding a
constant to all four entries. Two consecutive rows settle it, so the state is one row and the
engine is the predicate.

Pinned first, as always, and this time the obvious reading was right on the first try: 20 of the
20 entries small enough to count by hand came back exactly. 15 proved (the rest are square, too
wide, or carry no recurrence), all brute-forced from the words of the name — two of them by
enumerating rows rather than cells, their smallest array being too large for a full product.

### 6 September 2026, eighth pass — two more wordings, and an audit that cried wolf a third time

Two clusters, both refusals rather than new mathematics.

**"every one adjacent to another one"** (13 entries, none papered, none read by any engine). It
says exactly what `transfer71` already reads as "every 1 a horizontal or vertical neighbor to
some 1" — only the words differ. One pattern; 12 proved.

**Orientation.** `transfer41` reads `(n+1) X (W+k)` and nothing else, so the same family written
the other way round — `(6+1) X (n+1)`, the fixed side first — was invisible to every engine.
Transposing exchanges horizontal with vertical and FIXES both diagonals, so it is the same
problem with two words swapped. 6 proved. The transposed silent refusal was on the list from the
5 September audit ("30 transposed") and this is the first of them cleared.

**And the audit cried wolf again.** The regression pass over `transfer41`'s existing papers
reported three DATA MISMATCHES. All three were the harness: it called `transfer41.terms`
directly, which does not divide by the entry's fraction head, so "Half the number of ..." came
out exactly twice the data. Going through `uniform`, which does divide, all 73 pass.

That is the third false alarm from an audit's own bug in two days — the superscript one, the
comma one, and now the fraction one. The pattern is the same every time: **the check was written
against a different interface from the one the result was produced through.** The rule that
follows: an audit must go through the same interface the sweep does, or it is testing a
different claim.

18 proved in this pass. Roster 8762 → 8780. `audit_uni.py` clean at 2875 of 2875.

### 6 September 2026, ninth pass — a property of the nine cells of a 3 X 3 block: 28 proofs

`transfer75` reads five properties of a 3 X 3 window: its sum lying in a stated set, the
multiset of how often each value occurs, a positive determinant, the sum of the absolute
differences over all pairs of its entries, and "the same population". State is
`(u, v, carried)` — two rows and what the window condition has already forced — and the guard
`W < 3 or A ** W > 60000` is a function of the entry alone, never of the caller's cap.

**Three readings pinned against published data before a line of the engine was written.**

- "two of one value, three of another and four of the last" is the SORTED multiplicity list,
  not an assignment of values to counts.
- "72 absolute element differences equal to 34" counts the 36 UNORDERED pairs twice over; 34
  is not an achievable ordered-pair sum at all, and the unordered reading gives A234834's
  published 4032 exactly.
- "the same population" is the count of EACH value, not the sum of the entries.

**The last one was a latent bug in `transfer23`, and the DATA gate caught it.** The two
readings agree on every binary matrix, which is why the sum reading survived every binary
entry of that family. Over `0..2` it gives A224654 = 102789 where the entry publishes 67797.
23 hits made under the wrong reading were dropped and re-swept; the regression over the 39
existing `transfer23` papers came back 35 ok, 4 too big, 0 mismatch, and the three population
papers already in the roster are all binary, so their wording was right all along.

23 + 5 proved. Roster 8780 → 8808.

### 6 September 2026, tenth pass — nine proofs that were never written up, and 66 papers that said the opposite of their entry

Two findings, both from `audit_uni.py` rather than from new mathematics.

**Nine results sat proved and unpapered.** The per-engine paper builders read
`transfer<N>_hits.json`; the later unified sweep writes `uniall_hits.json`. Nine entries were
proved only by the second, at a cap the first had refused, so they lived in the unified file
with no paper and no roster slot: A228666, A228688, A228759 (`transfer9`), A229753
(`transfer16`), A255089, A255226, A255790, A255799, A256746 (`transfer17`). All nine
brute-forced from the English before anything was built — the three 7 X n binary arrays at
n = 1, 2, 3, the five 3 X 3 subblock entries at n = 1 by exhausting all 2^24 arrays of the
shape, and the defective-colouring entry at n = 1 and n = 2 — every value matching the entry.
Re-run through their own engines they proved again, and they are papers like any other.

**The lesson is the file, not the mathematics.** A result recorded in one place and read from
another is a result that quietly does not exist. Anything the unified sweep proves has to be
reconciled against the roster, not assumed to have flowed into it.

**And 66 papers stated the opposite of their entry.** For the `no 3 X 3 subblock ...` bodies
the parser rewrites the condition positively — `every diagonal sum \notin {0}` — so the
negation is already inside the displayed formula. `transfer17build` then wrapped that display
in the entry's own word: "holds for NO such g". Negated twice. The abstract carried the same
double negative. The mathematics and the model were never affected — the engine's predicate is
what counts, and it reproduces every published term — but 66 roster papers described their
object wrongly in prose, and 5 of the nine new ones would have too. Fixed by taking the
quantifier from the displayed formula rather than from the body word it was built from; all 71
rebuilt and recompiled, no LaTeX errors.

**Two `audit_uni.py` flags resolved, both benign.** A228688 and A228759 report "range not
tight": the recurrence also holds at the paper's stated threshold, so the claim understates
its own range by one step. The cause is structural, not sloppiness — the walk starts at two
lines, a(1) is counted outside the matrix by a separate one-row enumeration, and so the
residual `iota^T M^j q(M) tau` has no index for n = order + 1. The claim is correct as printed;
the extra step is simply outside what the matrix argument can reach.

**Recorded honestly: the page-count spread.** House style is 3–5 pages. Measured across the
roster: 64 papers are 2 pages (all of them low-order recurrences, where there is genuinely less
to say) and 6 run to 6 pages. Not fixed — padding a short proof to reach a page count is worse
than a short proof.

9 proved. Roster 8808 → 8817.

### 6 September 2026, eleventh pass — the clashing-pair family reopened, and a clause a column walk cannot read

**23 proofs, and one engine deleted.**

The census's largest untouched cluster was `no element x(i,j) adjacent to value m-x(i,j)`,
39 unpapered entries. The condition is a FORBIDDEN PAIR and symmetric, so it never needs a
cell's whole neighbourhood at once and one row is enough state, where `transfer41` carries an
ordered pair of rows and refuses these widths. I wrote that engine, pinned it against 51
already-proved entries, swept it, brute-forced 18 results, built and integrated the papers ---
and only then found that `transfer47` had done exactly this two weeks ago, same reduction, same
clauses. **The engine was a duplicate and was withdrawn along with its ten papers.** What was
actually new in it was the edge construction, and that was folded into `transfer47` instead:
which rows may follow a given one is a per-position condition, so it is a union of bitsets
rather than a scan over every pair of rows.

**The bigger win was lumping.** States with the same future may be merged without changing
`iota^T M^n tau`, and the annihilation test's length is governed by the state count, so this is
not a tidy-up, it is the difference between minutes and hours: 2022 states became 199, 4666
became 37, 8820 became 783. `lumpauto.py` does it by ordinary partition refinement. With both
changes `transfer47` proved **16** entries it had refused, including widths and alphabets that
were previously out of reach entirely.

**The lesson, recorded plainly: search the existing engines before writing a new one.** Grep the
wording, not the family name. Two hours went into rebuilding something that was already there,
and the only thing that saved it from being shipped twice was reading `transfer47`'s docstring
while looking for something else.

**And that docstring is where the real result came from.** It says `transfer47` refuses a
`W X n` entry that carries a precedence clause, because the walk runs across columns and does
NOT visit the cells in row major order, which is the order the clause is stated in. My duplicate
engine had accepted those entries by transposing the scan along with the array --- reading the
clause in COLUMN major order --- and my brute force made the same mistake, so the two agreed
with each other and both matched the entry's data. **A brute force that shares the engine's
misreading is not an independent check.** Checking against a brute force written in the
ORIGINAL frame found the error at once, on the four entries of the eight whose neighbour set
includes the diagonal.

`transfer77` handles those properly. The first occurrence of a value in row major order sits at
its least row and then its least column, so the walk carries each named value's least row and
the order those least rows were attained --- and two values with the same least row must have
reached it in different columns, since otherwise they would share a cell, so that order breaks
every tie. The one thing that cannot be done is pruning: a least row can still drop and reorder
the first occurrences retroactively, so the clause is a property of the finished array and is
tested only in the accepting states. **7 proved.**

**A sign error worth remembering.** An offset reaching into the PREVIOUS column names the same
pair as its negation reaching into the next one, and normalising every offset to the `+1` side
is not optional: without it `antidiagonally` is silently tested as `diagonally`. The DATA gate
caught it --- four of eight entries mismatched, and they were exactly the four whose direction
list contains both words.

23 proved. Roster 8817 → 8840.

**Left standing.** `transfer47`: A233216 (`nX7 0..5` with a four-value clause) needs more than
400 000 states before lumping. `transfer77`: A233087, A233104, A233220, A233221 --- the builds
run in a couple of minutes but the annihilation test does not fit in one foreground chunk.

### 6 September 2026, twelfth pass — the alphabet grows, not the shape: 6 proofs

Every array family in this roster so far fixes the alphabet and lets the shape grow, which is
what makes the count a walk in a finite digraph. `transfer78` is the first that goes the other
way: **`Number of K X K X K triangular 0..n arrays with some element plus some adjacent element
totalling n exactly once`** has a FIXED triangle of $T = K(K+1)/2$ cells, and $n$ is the size of
the alphabet. There is no digraph to walk and nothing about transfer matrices applies.

What works instead is inclusion--exclusion over the adjacent pairs. A set $S$ of pairs forces
$x_v = t - x_u$ along every edge of $S$, so within a connected component one value determines
all the rest by alternation; a component carrying an ODD cycle forces $2x=t$ and so admits one
value when $t$ is even and none otherwise. Hence

    N(S) = (n+1)^(T - touched) * B^(bipartite components) * F^(odd components)

with `B` a linear polynomial in `n` and `F` a function of `n` mod 2. Every exponent is
independent of `n`, so the sum over subsets is taken ONCE and every value of `a(n)` is then
free. The result is that **a(n) = A(n) + (-1)^n C(n) exactly, for every n >= 0, with no
threshold at all** --- a quasi-polynomial of period 2.

The recurrence is then not a computation but a division: a sequence of that shape is annihilated
by `(E-1)^(deg A+1) (E+1)^(deg C+1)` and by no proper divisor, and in all six entries the
conjectured recurrence's characteristic polynomial is EXACTLY that operator. Hardin's
recurrences here are minimal, not merely valid.

The same closed form settles the two `n mod 2` formulas each entry carries as separate
empirical lines: they are the quasi-polynomial read at each parity, and they agree to the
coefficient.

6 proved (K = 2, 3, 4 for each of the targets `n` and `n+1`). Roster 8840 → 8846.

**The wall is the subset sum, and it is sharp.** The triangle has `3*C(K,2)` adjacent pairs: 3,
9, 18, 30, 45, 63 for K = 2..7. At K = 5 that is 2^30 subsets, so A270260, A270261, A270262 and
A270513, A270514, A270515 are out of reach this way. The fix, if it is worth it, is a
connectivity DP across the triangle's rows carrying the boundary partition with parities and an
odd-cycle flag --- the boundary is at most K+1 cells, so the state count is small. Recorded, not
attempted.

**A category worth looking for.** Every entry whose SHAPE is fixed and whose alphabet is `0..n`
is a candidate for this treatment, and the roster has never gone after them. That is a whole
class, not one family.

### 6 September 2026, thirteenth pass — plane partitions in a box: 41 proofs, and the honest accounting

Acting on the note from the previous pass: **every entry whose SHAPE is fixed and whose alphabet
is `0..n` is a candidate**, and the roster had never gone after them. There are 619 unpapered
entries with a `0..n` alphabet. The largest single cluster is 42 entries reading

    Number of P X Q matrices with elements in 0..n with each row and each column in
    nondecreasing order.

Reverse the rows and the columns and a nondecreasing matrix becomes a nonincreasing one, which
is exactly a plane partition with parts at most `n` inside a `P X Q` rectangle. So `a(n)` is the
number of plane partitions in a `P x Q x n` box, and MacMahon's box theorem gives it. The triple
product TELESCOPES in its third index --- `prod_{k=1..r} (i+j+k-1)/(i+j+k-2) = (r+i+j-1)/(i+j-1)`
--- leaving `a(n) = prod_i prod_j (n+i+j-1)/(i+j-1)`, visibly a polynomial in `n` of degree
`P*Q`. No Ehrhart theory needed to see it.

**What is actually proved here, stated plainly.** The box count is classical, and Sela Fried
already recorded it on these entries in October 2023, citing Stanley. What was still open is the
entry's OWN expression, marked `(Empirical)` on all 41, which looks nothing like MacMahon's:
`prod_{i=0..P-1} binomial(s,n+i) i!/(s-i)^(P-1-i)` with `s = n+Q+P-1`. Clearing its denominator
turns the claim into an identity between two polynomials in `n` whose degrees are bounded by
inspection (numerator `PQ + P(P-1)/2`, denominator `P(P-1)/2`), so evaluating at that many points
PROVES it rather than sampling it. Where a generating function is also conjectured --- one entry,
A140901, Berselli 2012 --- polynomiality fixes the denominator as `(1-x)^(PQ+1)` and the
numerator is the finite differences, so it follows too.

**So: the mathematics that does the work is MacMahon's, not mine.** The papers say so in the
abstract. What they close is the entry's own formula, by an argument that is finite and exact
but not deep. Counted, because 41 entries stop being empirical; flagged, because a reader should
know where the weight sits.

41 proved. Roster 8846 → 8887.

**The class is far from exhausted.** Still unpapered with a `0..n` alphabet: ~290 entries of the
form `(n+k) X (W+j) arrays of permutations of 0..n*W+c with each element having ...` (the shape
and the alphabet grow together --- that is the array-permutation family, and `transfer73` may
already reach some of them), 11 `lower triangles of a K X K 0..n array`, 11 more triangular
`0..n` wordings, 8 `idempotent K X K 0..n matrices of rank r`, and a long tail.

### 6 September 2026, fourteenth pass — a condition that only ever compares two entries: 20 proofs

Third family in the fixed-shape, growing-alphabet class, and the cleanest yet:

    Number of lower triangles of a K X K 0..n array with each element differing from all of
    its <directions> neighbours by d [or less]

The condition constrains DIFFERENCES only, so adding a constant to every entry keeps an array
admissible. The arrays therefore fall into translation classes; a class whose entries span `s`
contributes exactly `max(0, n+1-s)` arrays with entries in `0..n`; and

    a(n) = sum over classes of max(0, n+1-s).

**The bound is what makes this a proof rather than an extrapolation.** Any two cells are joined
by a path of at most `D` edges, `D` the diameter of the neighbour graph, and each edge moves the
value by at most `d`, so no class has `s > d*D`. For `n >= d*D` every term is positive and
`a(n)` is EXACTLY linear. Two evaluations then pin it, and the threshold is known in advance
rather than read off a plateau. Nothing is fitted.

The counts themselves come from a frontier walk over the cells in row major order, keeping only
the entries a later cell can still see --- at most `K+1` of them for this shape --- so no array
is ever written down.

**Each entry carries up to three conjectures and all three fall together**: the closed form
`a(n) = A*n - B`, Colin Barker's generating function, and the recurrence
`a(n) = 2a(n-1) - a(n-2)`, which is just the statement that the second difference of a linear
function vanishes. 20 entries, 41 conjectural statements settled.

**A parser detail that was costing conjectures.** The shared g.f. parser looks for a bare
`G.f.:` and then refuses any body containing the word "empirical" --- but this family writes
`Empirical g.f.: ...`, so every one of those lines was invisible. Stripping the marker first
turned 20 entries with one settled statement each into 20 with up to three. **A refusal that
looks like "no generating function here" and is really "the line is spelled differently" is the
same silent-refusal failure the ledger has now recorded four times.**

Three shapes at K = 7 are too large to enumerate array by array for the independent check. Their
first term is argued exactly instead: at `n = 1` every entry is 0 or 1, so an "at most" condition
is no condition and the count is `2^T`, while "differing by exactly one" asks for a proper
2-colouring of the neighbour graph. Both test the cell set and the adjacency, which is what the
brute force exists to test.

20 proved. Roster 8887 → 8907.

### 6 September 2026, fifteenth pass — entries whose ONLY conjecture is a generating function: 44 proofs

**Every sweep in this repository gates on a parsable recurrence.** An entry whose only
conjecture is a generating function was therefore never examined at all --- not refused, never
reached. There are 162 such entries outside the roster and an engine already reads the name of
49 of them.

The argument is finite and exact. The model gives `a(n)` as a walk count on `S` states, so
`A(x) = N1/D1` with `D1 = det(I - xM)` of degree at most `S`. The conjecture says `A = N2/D2`.
Then `R = N1*D2 - N2*D1` is a polynomial of degree at most `S - 1 + deg D2`, and `A = N2/D2`
exactly when `R = 0` --- so comparing `S + deg N2 + deg D2 + 1` coefficients PROVES the
identity instead of testing it. 44 proved, 0 false, `S` from 15 to 16384.

**And each one yields a recurrence the entry does not record.** The denominator of a rational
generating function is a linear recurrence written backwards, so every one of these 44 entries
now has an explicit constant-coefficient recurrence valid past the numerator's degree. All 44
were checked against the entry's own published terms.

**This is the fifth silent refusal, and the widest one yet.** The shared g.f. parser looks for a
bare `G.f.:` and refuses any body containing the word "empirical". The corpus writes
`Empirical g.f.: ...`, `Conjecture: g.f. ...` and `Empirical: G.f.: ...`. **2837 entries carry
such a line and 2775 of them become parseable the moment the marker is stripped.** Most are
already papered by their recurrence, but the refusal was invisible and total.

**The brute force was wrong three times and the engines were right.** Writing the independent
check for the nine non-`transfer46` entries, I dropped clauses from three names --- the
neighbour list in two (`horizontally or antidiagonally`, which I had written as king moves) and
a canonical-form clause in the third (`new values introduced in order 0 sequentially upwards`,
which halves the count). All three disagreed with the model; in all three the CHECK was wrong.
That is the second time this session that the independent check has been the faulty side, and
it is worth stating plainly: a check is only worth what the care taken over it is worth.

44 proved. Roster 8907 → 8951.

**Left standing.** A250852 and A250876 exceed 200 000 states before merging. And 113 of the 162
g.f.-only entries have no engine reading their name at all --- that is the pool to go after
next, not a wall.

### Signals worth opening
Garbled or self-contradictory wording; an idle hypothesis (check whether the caveat is
load-bearing, or is a classical theorem's hypothesis in disguise); a contributor stating
several instances of one pattern; a homemade object with no literature; FORMULA
restating COMMENTS.

### Discipline that caught real errors
Write the verification script separately from the paper and print every number the paper
claims. Implement the core operation twice by different algorithms. Check the entry's
offset and first term before assuming the indexing.

## 6 September 2026, seventeenth pass — a sense the parser could not see, and a budget that rejected good results

23 proofs. Roster 9012 -> 9035.

**`transfer46` read both directions as nondecreasing, in the parser AND in the brute force.**
The family's names run `nondecreasing <f> in the i direction and nondecreasing <g> in the j
direction`, and six entries say NONINCREASING in the j direction. The parser's pattern spelled
both senses out literally, so those six were invisible; had they been visible, the edge test
hardcoded `>` in both directions and would have modelled them wrongly. Both now carry a sense
that travels with its statistic under transposition. Regression over the 220 existing
`transfer46` results: 207 reproduce their data, 0 wrong, 13 skipped for size.

**The sweep was rejecting good results because it asked for too few terms.** `sweep_gfonly.py`
computed how many series coefficients the generating-function argument needs, then fetched that
many model terms and compared them against the entry's DATA. An entry publishing MORE terms
than the coefficient budget was therefore compared against a truncated list and recorded as
`model does not match DATA` --- when the model in fact matched every published term. A250737
matched all 31 of its terms and was thrown out. Fixed by asking for whichever is longer.
**Re-running everything the bug could have touched recovered 19 results.** A false negative
that reads exactly like a real one is worth more scrutiny than a false positive.

**Fourth and fifth times this session the independent check was the faulty side.**
`bf46.py` hardcoded the same sense the parser did, so it disagreed with the model on all five
mixed-sense entries; fixed, all five match. And for A203175 none of four readings I tried
reproduced the data, while the engine matched all 38 terms --- because `preceded by 0 1` means
the two cells to the left, or the two above, read 0 then 1 IN THAT ORDER, a two-step lookback,
not a condition on the immediate predecessors. Implemented independently, it reproduces the
entry exactly.

Five for five this session. The pattern is now unambiguous and belongs in the methodology: the
slow engine, written against the entry with its data as a gate, keeps being right; the quick
check written afterwards keeps being the sloppy one. A check is worth what the care taken over
it is worth, and these were written in a hurry precisely because they were "just" checks.

## 6 September 2026, eighteenth pass — a table sweep that had been refusing 62 of 71 engines

83 proofs. Roster 9035 -> 9115.

**`sweep_table.py` dispatched per engine by hand and called `<engine>.avals`, which 62 of the
71 engines do not have.** The `AttributeError` was swallowed by a broad `except` and reported
as `model does not match the column`, so every table whose column model came from one of those
engines was rejected as if the mathematics had failed. This is the same failure as the
`transfer7` one already in this ledger and the same fix: go through `uniform`, the shared
interface, instead of re-implementing the dispatch. Rewritten, and all 1330 previously examined
tables reopened and re-examined; 3 tables and 5 columns recovered. Smaller than feared, because
most of these tables state no explicit column recurrence at all.

**What they state instead is `[order N]`, and that is a claim.** 619 tables carry such lines,
1095 of them outside the roster. `sweep_ordline.py` settles them: a column is a fixed-width
array count, hence a walk count on S vertices, hence satisfies a monic recurrence of order at
most S; Berlekamp--Massey on 2S exact terms returns the minimal one; if its order is the stated
one then every recurrence of that order the column satisfies is that same polynomial. **The
sweep had been run at a state cap of 1200, which was refusing most of them.** Re-run at 6000:
proved tables 43 -> 123, recovered lines 55 -> 197, of which **80 tables and 142 lines are
new**. The independent re-check passed 123 of 123 with no problems.

**The cap was not a wall, it was a setting**, and nothing recorded that it had been chosen
rather than reached. Worth a rule: when a sweep reports `state space > cap`, the cap is part of
the result and belongs in the ledger next to it.

**Length now follows content here.** These papers come out at two pages when one column was
recovered and three when several were, which is what it should look like.

**Left standing.** 24 entries of the `nondecreasing ... i direction` family are `(n+1)X(n+1)`,
both sides growing --- the n X n wall, a real obstruction. Of the remaining order-line tables,
those still refused sit above 6000 states.

### transfer81 — arrays counted up to renaming, under a subblock condition (36 entries)

A family of 46 Hardin entries that no engine parsed. Each asks two things at once: a
condition on every 2×2 or 3×3 subblock, and "new values introduced in row major order".
The second is not a local condition — whether a value may appear here depends on the whole
prefix — but the prefix enters only through **how many values have been introduced so far**,
so one extra integer in the state carries it exactly. 36 proved; the other 10 carry no
conjecture at all and are not counted.

Four readings pinned against published DATA before the engine was written, one per
predicate shape, each by a program enumerating arrays from the entry's own words.

**The mistake.** The parser treated `L X (n+a)` as the transpose of `(n+a) X L`. It is not:
the conditions are stated about ROWS — "every subblock in a row", "adjacent rows differing",
"row major order" — so transposing rewrites the condition into a different one. Six entries
were reported as "model does not match DATA", which is the only reason it was caught; had
those six been absent the error would have shipped. The fix walks the array along its own
growing direction and keeps the conditions where the entry puts them.

That fix needed one real argument rather than a code change alone. Walking by columns, the
canonical condition read along the walk is *column* major order, not the entry's row major
order. They give the same count: every condition here is a statement about which entries are
equal, so it is invariant under renaming the values, and each rule picks exactly one
representative from each renaming class. Checked, not assumed — an independent brute force
written to the entry's row-major wording reproduces the published terms of A205627.

Thirty of these had already been papered and ranked when the defect turned up. The natural
orientation was not touched by the fix, but "not touched" is a claim about code and the
roster is a claim about mathematics, so all 36 were re-run from scratch through the shipped
engine (`src/reverify81.py`) and every paper rebuilt from that run.

**Cap recorded next to the refusal:** A206173 refused at cap 6000 with "state space > cap",
and settled at cap 400000. Its lumped model has 76 states.
